با این حال، این شرکت که توسعه‌دهنده چت‌بات هوش مصنوعی «کلود»  است در ماه‌های پیش رو همچنان زیر ذره‌بین خواهد بود تا به این پرسش کلیدی پیرامون هوش مصنوعی پاسخ دهد: آیا تمام این هزینه‌ها ارزشش را دارد؟

در همان ساعات نخست معاملات، به نظر می‌رسید سهام آنتروپیک نشان می‌دهد که سرمایه‌گذاران هنوز نسبت به مسیر دقیق آینده هوش مصنوعی اطمینان ندارند. قیمت هر سهم بلافاصله تا ۱۱۱/۵ دلار بالا رفت و ارزش بازار شرکت را به نزدیک ۲ تریلیون دلار رساند، اما پیش از پایان روز کاهش یافت و به ۹۷ دلار رسید.

برخی سرمایه‌گذاران معتقد بودند که عرضه اولیه آنتروپیک موفقیت‌آمیز بوده است، چرا که قیمت سهام در طول روز حدود ۱۷ درصد افزایش یافت؛ هرچند عملکرد کلی بازار فناوری به آن خوبی نبود.

شاخص ترکیبی نزدک که عمدتاً شامل شرکت‌های فناوری است، با کاهشی نزدیک به ۲/۳ درصد به کار خود پایان داد. ارزش سهام بزرگ‌ترین شرکت‌های فناوری، از جمله «آلفابت» (شرکت مادر گوگل) با ۳ درصد افت و «آمازون» با ۳/۹ درصد افت، کاهش یافت.

توسعه زیرساخت‌ها در عصر کنونی هوش مصنوعی، یکی از پرهزینه‌ترین اقدامات در تاریخ فناوری محسوب می‌شود؛ به‌طوری که تنها در سال گذشته، بیش از یک تریلیون دلار توسط تعداد انگشت‌شماری از شرکت‌های بزرگ فناوری هزینه شده است.

سرعت رشد سرمایه‌گذاری‌ها موجب بروز نگرانی‌هایی مداوم در مورد شکل‌گیری یک «حباب مالی» شده است.

ریچارد ویتل، اقتصاددان دانشگاه سالفورد، می‌گوید: «حباب‌ها در روز انجام بزرگ‌ترین معامله نمی‌ترکند؛ بلکه زمانی می‌ترکند که چشم‌انداز مثبت آینده، مورد تردید قرار گیرد.»

منبع تصویر، Leonardo MUNOZ / AFP via Getty Images

گزیده‌ای از مهم‌ترین خبرها، گزارش‌های میدانی و گفت‌وگوهای اختصاصی را هر هفته در ایمیل خود دریافت کنید.

اگرچه اصول اولیه این فناوری دهه‌هاست که وجود دارد، اما ظهور اخیر رایانه‌های قدرتمندتر و تراشه‌های مرتبط با آن‌ها، امکان پردازش حجم بی‌سابقه‌ای از داده‌ها را فراهم کرده است.

نتیجه این تحول، پیدایش چت‌بات‌های هوش مصنوعی بوده است که گفتار انسان را شبیه‌سازی می‌کنند و وظایفی همچون کدنویسی نرم‌افزار، تولید تصاویر دیجیتال و جستجو در اینترنت را با سرعتی بسیار بالا انجام می‌دهند.

این پدیده نشان‌دهنده شیوه جدیدی در به‌کارگیری رایانه‌هاست که به رشد سریع شرکت «آنتروپیک» منجر شده است؛ شرکتی که تنها پنج سال پیش تأسیس شد و بیشتر به عنوان سازنده چت‌بات محبوب هوش مصنوعی، «کلود» شناخته می‌شود.

به گفته بن بارینجر، مدیر بخش تحقیقات فناوری در شرکت «کوئیلتر چویوت»، آنتروپیک به عنوان نخستین شرکتی که تمام‌وکمال بر پایه هوش مصنوعی بنا شده و وارد بازار سهام می‌شود، به‌احتمال‌زیاد در آینده شاهد نوسانات قابل‌توجهی در قیمت سهام خود خواهد بود.

بارینجر با اشاره به آنچه اوایل امسال برای شرکت اسپیس‌ایکس رخ داد، می‌گوید که آن «شور و هیجان اولیه» به‌تدریج فروکش خواهد کرد.

سهام شرکت اسپیس‌اکس، به رهبری ایلان ماسک، در نخستین روز عرضه حدود ۱۰ درصد جهش کرد و ارزش‌گذاری این شرکت را به رقم بی‌سابقه ۲/۲ تریلیون دلار رساند.

اما ظرف یک ماه، قیمت سهام اسپیس‌ایکس به کمتر از قیمت روز عرضه اولیه رسید و پس از آن نیز عمدتاً به روند نزولی خود ادامه داد.

سهام بسیاری از شرکت‌های فناوری پس از ورود به بازار بورس، به‌ویژه زمانی که برای نخستین بار گزارش عملکرد سه‌ماهه خود را منتشر می‌کنند، با افت قیمت مواجه می‌شوند.

با این حال، بسیاری از همین شرکت‌ها، از جمله متا، آمازون و گوگل، در ادامه مسیر به بزرگ‌ترین و سودآورترین شرکت‌های جهان تبدیل شده‌اند.

در مورد آنتروپیک، سرمایه‌گذاران نه تنها با یک شرکت فناوری برجسته با ارزش‌گذاری کلان و آینده‌ای تجاری که می‌تواند بسیار درخشان باشد روبرو هستند، بلکه با شرکتی مواجه‌اند که در نوع خود نخستین نمونه‌ای است که پا به بازار سهام می‌گذارد.

نیل ویلسون، استراتژیست سرمایه‌گذاری در شعبه بریتانیای کارگزاری ساکسو می‌گوید: «هیچ همتای مشخصی وجود ندارد که بتوان آنتروپیک را با آن مقایسه کرد.»

بنابراین، وقتی سرمایه‌گذاران خرد و حتی پژوهشگران و سرمایه‌گذاران صندوق‌های بزرگ مالی از خود می‌پرسند که آیا آنتروپیک واقعاً ۱/۵ تریلیون دلار (یا حتی بیشتر) ارزش دارد، پاسخ‌های چندانی برای این پرسش نخواهند یافت.

ویلسون می‌گوید: «ما می‌توانیم حدس‌هایی بزنیم، اما گمان نمی‌کنم کسی واقعاً پاسخ دقیق را بداند.»

احتمالاً عوامل چندی بر موفقیت این شرکت در بازار سهام طی کوتاه‌مدت تأثیرگذار خواهند بود.

یکی از این موارد، چشم‌انداز قوانین جدید حاکم بر استفاده از ابزارهای هوش مصنوعی است. در ایالات متحده، جایی که شرکت آنتروپیک مستقر است، دموکرات‌ها تا سال ۲۰۲۷ در مناصب قدرت بسیار بیشتری قرار خواهند گرفت و چندین سیاستمدار پیش از این گفته بودند که به دنبال اطمینان از ایمن بودن ابزارهای هوش مصنوعی و نصب برخی محافظ‌ها خواهند بود.

بر اساس سندی که در تاریخ ۱۰ نوامبر به کمیسیون بورس و اوراق بهادار نیویوک ارائه شده است، هم‌بنیان‌گذاران این شرکت، شامل داریو و دانیلا آمودی، تام براون، جک کلارک، جرد کاپلان، سم مک‌کندلیش و کریس اولا، هر کدام صاحب حدود ۲۴۰ تا ۲۴۴ میلیون سهم از این شرکت هستند.

با توجه به قیمت پایانی امروز، یعنی ۹۷/۱۷ دلار برای هر سهم، ارزش سهام هر یک از این بنیان‌گذاران بین ۲۳/۳ میلیارد دلار تا ۲۳/۷ میلیارد دلار برآورد می‌شود.

مدیران شرکت، از جمله داریو آمودی، از بنیانگذاران و مدیرعامل آنتروپیک، در مورد ترس‌های خود مبنی بر اینکه ابزارهای هوش مصنوعی آینده آنقدر توانمند شوند که از انسان‌ها پیشی بگیرند، تا جایی که انقراض کامل انسان ممکن باشد، صریحاً ابراز نگرانی کرده‌اند.

آنتروپیک همیشه خود را به عنوان یک شرکت هوش مصنوعی که ایمنی فناوری خود را بسیار جدی می‌گیرد، در چشم عموم مطرح کرده است.

دانیلا آمودی، رئیس شرکت آنتروپیک و خواهر داریو آمودی، روز پنجشنبه با افتخار اعلام کرد که این شرکت «قبل از عرضه اولین محصول خود، یک تیم ایمنی هوش مصنوعی داشت».

او افزود: «هوش مصنوعی خطرات واقعی را به همراه دارد.»

با وجود ادعاهای این شرکت مبنی بر اینکه فناوری هوش مصنوعی که با سرعت بالایی در حال ساخت آن است می‌تواند خطرناک باشد، آنتروپیک یکی از سریع‌ترین مسیرها را از زمان راه‌اندازی تا عرضه اولیه سهام در تاریخ شرکت‌ها طی کرده است.

A brazen cargo crook who helped steal nearly $100 million in jewelry after tailing a Brink’s truck across California has pleaded guilty, facing up to 20 years in federal prison.

Carlos Victor Mestanza Cercado, 33, an Ecuadorian national and lead defendant, admitted to the July 2022 heist, in which his crew busted the locks on a Brink’s semitruck at a Lebec truck stop and made off with 24 bags of jewelry valued at approximately $100 million.

The gang had tracked the truck from an international jewelry show in San Mateo, following it roughly 300 miles before striking in the early hours of July 11, 2022.

The thieves hauled their loot to East Hollywood to split up and sell. The multimillion-dollar score was part of a wider cargo-theft spree.

Mestanza also admitted to stealing more than $240,000 in Samsung electronics from a truck in Ontario and Apple AirTags worth $57,377 from a shipment in Fontana.

During the AirTags robbery, an accomplice threatened the truck driver with a knife.

The crew also stole another $14,081 in Samsung electronics from trucks in Fontana.

After a federal grand jury indicted him, Mestanza fled the US in June 2025.

He was arrested July 1 at Panama City’s Tocumen International Airport during a layover from Guatemala to Ecuador and extradited to the US.

He has been in federal custody since August 2025.

Authorities estimate restitution in the case to be at least $100,312,031.

Mestanza pleaded guilty to interference with commerce by robbery under the Hobbs Act.

US District Judge Kenly Kiya Kato scheduled sentencing for April 15, 2027.

He faces up to 20 years behind bars.

Three co-defendants have pleaded not guilty and are scheduled for trial March 22, 2027.

Carlos Victor Mestanza Cercado, 33, an Ecuadorian national and lead defendant, admitted to the July 2022 heist, in which his crew busted the locks on a Brink’s semitruck at a Lebec truck stop and made off with 24 bags of jewelry valued at approximately $100 million.

The gang had tracked the truck from an international jewelry show in San Mateo, following it roughly 300 miles before striking in the early hours of July 11, 2022.

The thieves hauled their loot to East Hollywood to split up and sell. The multimillion-dollar score was part of a wider cargo-theft spree.

Mestanza also admitted to stealing more than $240,000 in Samsung electronics from a truck in Ontario and Apple AirTags worth $57,377 from a shipment in Fontana.

During the AirTags robbery, an accomplice threatened the truck driver with a knife.

The crew also stole another $14,081 in Samsung electronics from trucks in Fontana.

After a federal grand jury indicted him, Mestanza fled the US in June 2025.

He was arrested July 1 at Panama City’s Tocumen International Airport during a layover from Guatemala to Ecuador and extradited to the US.

He has been in federal custody since August 2025.

Authorities estimate restitution in the case to be at least $100,312,031.

Mestanza pleaded guilty to interference with commerce by robbery under the Hobbs Act.

US District Judge Kenly Kiya Kato scheduled sentencing for April 15, 2027.

He faces up to 20 years behind bars.

Three co-defendants have pleaded not guilty and are scheduled for trial March 22, 2027.

“Actions that should raise alarm bells for $800, Alex.”

A sketchy project in Fairfield, Calif., could populate an entire “Jeopardy!” category.

The Fairfield City Council this week quietly approved a deal to let a Chinese-owned company set up operations in town, slurp up millions of gallons of city water — and, incredibly, install itself just 7 miles from a US Air Force base.

The biggest news, opinion and culture shaping California right now.

Please provide a valid email.

By clicking above you agree to the Terms of Use and Privacy Policy.

The action has triggered a public outcry, and worst of all: The city avoided US national-security review of the project.

That’s dangerous — abhorrent, even — and the council should reverse course immediately and insist on full federal review by the Committee on Foreign Investment in the United States.

The city’s approach has instead been unseemly.

Per Cat Moy, Fairfield’s former mayor, the deal was structured to duck federal review: The land was sold not directly to Nongfu Spring — owned by China’s second-richest man — but instead to a US middleman that would lease the property to a Nongfu Spring subsidiary.

And when Fairfield’s current vice mayor, Pam Bertani, questioned the no-review approach at this week’s council meeting, the city’s attorney scolded her:

“I think even talking about it now, you’re probably going to draw some media attention to this, and this administration may take it out on you all, and I can’t protect you from that,” said David Lim. Lim reportedly has since resigned as the city’s legal counsel, for undisclosed reasons.

The city also provided little to no opportunity for public input as the project was negotiated and prepared for approval; hence the outcry now.

If those alarm bells weren’t enough, there’s more:

The same Chinese company, Nongfu Spring, in 2025 pursued but paused (amid scrutiny) similar plans for a beverage facility in Nashua, NH. The state’s governor and a New Hampshire congresswoman demanded federal and state review of that project — which had been planned near a large US defense contractor, an FAA air traffic control center and other sensitive infrastructure.

Is it coincidence that a massive Chinese company has chosen more than one project site near US military and strategic assets?

And sadly, it’s unlikely that Gov. Gavin Newsom will be of help in the Fairfield case, as his administration helped facilitate Fairfield’s quiet deal.

At best, Fairfield officials put parochial concerns — including millions of dollars in city water sales to the Chinese beverage titan — above the safety of Americans.

As Moy told the California Post: “We do need the jobs, we do need the money — but you don’t sell out your nation for that.”

If the project is legit, why not submit it for national-security review? CFIUS, run by the Treasury Department, scrutinizes exactly this type of foreign investment for possible national security risks.

City officials said the project sits outside the radius of required reviews and that Chinese firm planned to seek voluntary federal scrutiny.

That’s light years from good enough. The city should err on the side of US security, and demand CFIUS review — not rely on the goodwill of a company connected to the United States’ leading foreign adversary.

Fairfield residents find all of this galling, as well they should.

Six of the city’s seven council members voted for this shady parochial deal — despite taking an oath to the US Constitution as a condition of serving in public office.

Their loyalty must be to the safety of Americans first and always, and not to local economic concerns, however pressing the latter may seem.

Whatever the council’s intentions may be, this could not be a worse look for Fairfield.

news.originalContent:

A San Diego transit worker exposed to 12,000 volts while working at a rail substation has died, triggering a workplace safety investigation.

Patrick Pryor, a veteran employee of the San Diego Metropolitan Transit System, died late on Nov. 13 after suffering severe electrical injuries at the agency’s 33rd and K Street substation, according to a friend who spoke with FOX 5/KUSI.

Pryor’s coworkers, emergency responders and hospital medical professionals tried to save him. He died surrounded by loved ones, MTS CEO Sharon Cooney told employees.

California’s Division of Occupational Safety and Health is investigating the fatal accident. MTS has not identified what caused the electrical exposure.

“The cause of this tragic accident has not yet been determined,” Cooney wrote to FOX 5/KUSI. “We are committed to understanding what happened and taking appropriate steps to prevent similar tragedies.”

Pryor had worked for MTS since 2006, becoming a Wayside Electromechanic in 2011. He also helped train apprentices in the agency’s rail Maintenance of Way department.

His death has devastated coworkers, with one longtime friend describing the loss as potentially the first fatality of its magnitude in the department’s history.

The friend, who requested anonymity, said Pryor was known for his expertise, steady temperament and willingness to take on additional work. He was someone colleagues could count on, the friend told FOX 5/KUSI.

MTS said it is cooperating with Cal/OSHA and other investigating authorities. The agency has also made crisis counselors available to employees, offering confidential support around the clock.

9-1-1 did the thing! And by that, we mean ABC’s hit first responder drama once again left fans fearing for Athena Grant’s life and THE Angela Bassett’s future on the show.

Spoilers for 9-1-1 Season 10, Episode 6 ahead.

9-1-1 Season 10, Episode 6, “Et Tu?” was an eventful hour that featured emergencies, a long-awaited Eddie (Ryan Guzman) and Maddie (Jennifer Love Hewitt) scene, an unexpected one-night stand, and Buck (Oliver Stark) and Eddie’s highly anticipated makeup. But right before 9-1-1 embarked on its weeks-long hiatus, the midseason finale ended on a tragic cliffhanger involving our favorite 9-1-1 detective.

Naturally, with 9-1-1 on hiatus until January 7, 2027, fans will be fearing for Athena. So does Athena die in 9-1-1 Season 10? And is Angela Bassett leaving 9-1-1? Ultimately, we’ll have to tune in and see, but here are our thoughts about Athena’s 9-1-1 fate after the mid-season finale.

9-1-1 Season 10, Episode 6, “Et Tu?” kicked off with Athena learning that Detective Ben Hooks — the man who shot her in Season 9 — was dead. Because he was fatally injured in the prison yard, police were investigating anyone with motive to kill, so Athena was advised to get a good lawyer ahead of questioning.

With minutes left in the episode, we heard Athena coughing and throwing up in the bathroom ahead of her interrogation. When a woman at the sinks asked what was wrong, Athena blamed her sickness on “too much coffee,” saying, “it turns my stomach into battery acid.” Athena headed into a room to meet her lawyer, who instantly clocked her sweat and weak demeanor. She told him she was sleep-deprived and anxious, but when he suggested they reschedule the questioning, she protested, saying, “No, no, no. I don’t want to drag this out any longer. I’ll rally.”

As two officers (one being the woman from the bathroom) interrogated Athena, she repeatedly grabbed her neck as if she were in pain. And when the questioning became more intense, Athena’s lawyer jumped in to remind the officers that “Ben Hooks was a crooked police officer who murdered at least one man in cold blood while also attempting the murder of a fellow colleague.”

Even though she clearly felt sick, Athena refused to lie when asked about her negative feelings towards Hooks. So the officers continued to sling accusations, calling her angry and vengeful. Tensions rose, and when they pulled out a photo of an inmate they believed to be the inside man who killed Hooks, Athena’s vision blurred, her hearing dulled, and she collapsed to the floor. Before the end credits rolled, her lawyer said, “I think she’s having a heart attack. Someone call 9-1-1.” So while Athena’s fate is a mystery until JANUARY 2027 (!!!), we do have some thoughts about Bassett’s future on the show.

Is Athena dead? Is Angela Bassett leaving 9-1-1? Fans never imagined the show without Bobby Nash and Peter Krause, and we all know what happened there. So unfortunately, never say never! But I’ve said it before, and I’ll say it again: I, for one, can’t imagine 9-1-1 killing another core character — especially MS. ATHENA GRANT NASH — this soon after Bobby’s death. Doing that to viewers? The 118? Athena’s kids? I mean, it’s downright diabolical. Plus, if you think Queen Athena would ever go out by something as common as a heart attack (especially after Bobby’s grand heroic death), I simply can’t relate!

Minear once told TV Fanatic he’s “a little superstitious about having an episode that doesn’t have [Athena] in it,” so hopefully that means Bassett isn’t going anywhere and this latest scare simply means we’ll get some intense, emotional scenes of May and the 118 at the hospital. Athena just became a detective, and she’s a critical, complex character, friend, and parent who regularly makes the impossible possible and absolutely shines in big emergency episodes. Fans would straight-up riot if the show lost Bassett, and the series is an incredible showcase for her talents. So, again, I don’t think 9-1-1 is going to put fans and characters through the wringer again by killing the show’s biggest star.

That said, fans are still going to be on edge counting down the days until 9-1-1 returns next year!

Stay tuned for more 9-1-1 coverage from Decider.

9-1-1 returns with new episodes on Thursday, Jan 7, 2027.

First lady Melania Trump dazzled in an elegant Dolce & Gabbana black dress as she premiered her new two-part docuseries on the world stage in Manhattan Thursday night — close on the heels of her chart-topping self-titled documentary.

“Melania, The Series” — comprised of two episodes — made its silver screen debut at Lincoln Center’s Alice Tully Hall, a day before it drops in more than 240 countries on Prime Video.

Melania took to the red carpet along with former US Attorney General Pam Bondi, her partner John Wakefield, ex-Trump White House senior adviser Kellyanne Conway and others.

The first lady told reporters that the series “was very exciting to do” but noted it “was a lot of work” and “not an easy task.”

“It was the first time I was involved from the idea till the end,” Melania said. “Everything what you see, it’s my idea. From the advertising, from the music, editing”

Conway praised the first lady and pointed out how frequently she offers advice to President Trump.

“She is a very trusted adviser to him, as well as, obviously, his wife and his partner,” Conway said of Melania. “She’s been my friend for many years.”

The first lady’s new series reveals never-told-before stories of President Trump’s 56-year-old wife and pulls back the curtain on the immediate aftermath of the 47th presidential inauguration in January 2025.

Melania told “Fox & Friends” earlier this year that the series will be “very different” to “Melania, The Documentary,” which followed the first lady throughout the 20 days leading up to her husband’s second inauguration.

“It’s more conversation one-on-one with me,” she said in September. “There’s some private questions that I will answer that people never heard before, so it’s kind of exciting.”

The first episode, titled “Family & Trust” focuses on Melania preparing to once again become America’s first lady but inside the walls of the White House, trust is tested and Melania “must protect those closest to her while navigating the demands of power.”

Jax Taylor shared a “graphic” photo of his tumor after undergoing surgery on his kidney amid his cancer battle.

“I know this is a bit graphic, but I can’t tell you how much I am relieved this is out of me,” he wrote via his Instagram Stories Thursday.

“Hoping they have gotten it all.”

Taylor, 47, candidly posted his tumor after he went public with his cancer diagnosis hours prior.

“This is something I’ve kept private for the past few months because it’s been one of the scariest times of my life,” the “Vanderpump Rules” alum wrote alongside a photo of himself in a hospital bed.

The reality star reflected on initially going to the hospital in July, believing he had kidney stones.

However, the visit “turned into something [he] never imagined.”

“My CT scan also showed a tumor on my left kidney,” Taylor added. “After many tests and appointments, I found out it was cancer.”

The Bravo star explained the tumor, which was “a lot larger than [doctors] thought,” had been removed after a five-hour surgery, and they were “waiting on the pathology results.”

news.originalContent:
Rising data center energy needs force Meta to adjust its sustainability targets amid growing corporate climate retreat.

Meta, the owner of Facebook and Instagram, has said it is reconsidering its 2030 deadline for reaching net-zero emissions because of the artificial intelligence (AI) boom, in the latest sign of a broad corporate retreat from climate pledges.

The company is “re-evaluating our timelines, sequencing and interim milestones, including the 2030 timeframe for our net zero emissions goal”, Rachel Peterson, Meta’s vice president of data centres, and Blair Swedeen, its global head of net zero and sustainability, said in the company’s annual sustainability report on Thursday.

Meta reported that its net carbon-equivalent emissions rose 45 percent in 2025 to 11.8 million tonnes, a figure that is itself based on accounting methods that climate advocates view with scepticism.

“When we set our net zero emissions goal, we anticipated steady growth, falling clean energy costs, and changes in the broader system that would enable progress at the pace we envisioned. The reality has been far more complex,” the executives wrote in the report. They said delivering on Meta’s vision “requires building the infrastructure that powers AI”.

In 2020, Meta set a goal of net-zero emissions across its entire value chain by 2030, in line with the Paris Agreement, which aims to hold long-term warming to 1.5C (2.7F) above pre-industrial levels.

Net zero means eliminating emissions as far as possible and buying credits from carbon removal projects to offset those that cannot be eliminated. The value chain covers emissions from sources such as purchased goods and services, as well as capital goods such as equipment, buildings and vehicles.

A study published this week in the journal Nature Sustainability found that 403 of the most powerful data centres in the United States accounted for about 2 percent of the country’s electricity use and a carbon footprint comparable to Denmark’s, the AFP news agency reported.

About 1,200 such “hyperscale” data centres are online, and hundreds more are planned. Globally, data centres used about 415 terawatt hours of electricity in 2024, about 1.5 percent of supply, and that could nearly double by 2030, according to the International Energy Agency.

During US President Donald Trump’s second term, major American businesses have stepped back from environmental commitments.

The trend is not confined to Big Tech. General Motors, which set a goal of selling only zero-emission vehicles by 2035, backed the Trump administration’s weakening of a fuel economy rule this year.

Walmart acknowledged in 2024 that it would miss its first emissions target. Google, which pledged in 2020 to run on carbon-free energy by 2030, said this year that its emissions were still rising.

Coca-Cola and Pepsi have changed the baseline years for their emissions targets and weakened their ambitions.

news.originalContent:
Three top Democrats called Trump’s dealings with law firms a case of ‘official coercion’ and pledged investigations.

Democrats in the United States say their investigation has revealed that the law firm Kirkland & Ellis provided at least $11.8m in free legal work to President Donald Trump’s administration.

On Thursday, Representative Jamie Raskin, Senator Richard Blumenthal and Senator Adam Schiff released a statement calling the sum evidence of Trump’s “unprecedented official coercion of major law firms”.

Since Trump returned to the White House for a second term, he has issued executive orders seeking to bar certain law firms from receiving security clearances and government contracts.

His administration has also threatened law firms with workplace discrimination investigations. Those orders and probes have led some of the firms to enter into settlements with the Trump administration, offering millions of dollars in free services.

“We have recently received substantial and profoundly troubling information that this corrupt bargain went much further than originally understood,” the three Democrats said in the statement, citing the $11.8m in services.

They proceeded to request records from nine other law firms, in an effort to determine if they too had done free work on behalf of the Trump administration.

“Since April 2025, the lawmakers have repeatedly demanded answers about the ten firms’ dubious multimillion-dollar deals with President Trump,” the statement said.

“However, to date, the vast majority of the firms still have yet to provide any substantive answers or turn over a single responsive document.”

The three Democrats involved in Thursday’s statement include lawmakers poised to take leadership roles in investigations during the upcoming 120th Congress.

The Democratic Party won control of both chambers of Congress in the November 3 midterm elections.

That will give the party power over Congress’s ability to oversee investigations and issue subpoenas. The new Congress is slated to be sworn in on January 3.

Raskin is currently the ranking member of the House Judiciary Committee. Blumenthal, meanwhile, is the ranking member of the Senate’s Permanent Subcommittee on Investigations.

Schiff, for his part, gained fame for leading Trump’s first impeachment trial in 2020, over allegations that the president abused his power by seeking Ukraine’s help for his first re-election bid. Trump has previously called for Schiff’s prosecution.

The three Democrats say they received information about Kirkland & Ellis’s free services for the Trump administration two days after the midterm race.

Some $4m in services was reportedly offered to the Department of Commerce. Another $2.2m went to the Department of Defense, and $1.6m was dedicated to the US Postal Service.

Kirkland & Ellis also reportedly gave $2m in services to the US International Development Finance Corporation, an agency that provides loans and development assistance to overseas projects.

The Democrats also said $1.8m went to an “investment entity negotiated between the Trump Administration and Japan to create a $550 billion slush fund”.

In 2025, Kirkland & Ellis agreed to settle with the Trump administration after the Equal Employment Opportunity Commission (EEOC) opened an investigation into the law firm’s employment practices.

It accused Kirkland & Ellis of embracing diversity, equity and inclusion (DEI), a slogan for building greater opportunities for under-represented groups in education and the workplace.

The Trump administration, however, has characterised DEI as illegal discrimination, disadvantaging men and white people.

“The EEOC is prepared to root out discrimination anywhere it may rear its head, including in our nation’s elite law firms,” the commission’s acting chair said at the time.

In a Truth Social post on April 11, 2025, Trump revealed that Kirkland & Ellis had pledged $125m in free services. He also indicated that the EEOC would halt its investigation as a result.

Other law firms likewise entered into agreements to avoid the consequences of Trump’s executive actions or employment-related probes.

Estimates indicate that they collectively pledged nearly $1bn in pro bono services.

The handful of law firms that fought Trump’s executive orders, however, won their cases, with judges ruling the president’s actions to be unconstitutional.

In the case involving the law firm Perkins Coie, Judge Beryl Howell said the executive order against it was an “overt attempt to suppress and punish certain viewpoints”.

The Democrats in Thursday’s statement highlighted other concerns with the agreements.

The deals, they said, were announced on Truth Social, Trump’s social media platform. That made “the President the sole judge of whether those firms were complying with their obligations – putting these firms at the political mercy of the Administration”.

The Democrats also warned that law firms like Kirkland & Ellis might be dissuaded from taking on certain clients, for fear of upsetting Trump.

“For people and communities who rely on pro bono lawyers to defend their rights, that could mean facing the full power and intensifying fury of the federal government alone,” they said.

In a November letter obtained by the Reuters news agency, Kirkland said it began negotiating with the Trump administration after rival firm Skadden reached its own deal in March 2025.

It added that its White House agreement has had “little impact” on its pro bono work, telling lawmakers that the firm “still devotes substantial pro bono resources to interests that could be considered ‘progressive'”.

The law firm is represented by prominent Washington litigator Beth Wilkinson of Wilkinson Stekloff. She did not immediately respond to Reuters’s request for comment.

news.originalContent:
Motorists and businesses struggle as shortages disrupt daily life.

Blantyre, Malawi – Finding fuel in Malawi has become a daily struggle, with motorists spending hours, sometimes entire nights, waiting for tankers that may never arrive.

As shortages persist, filling stations across the country have become flashpoints for frustration and violence as motorists compete for dwindling supplies.

Ken Mhango, 40, a car flipper in Blantyre, recently drove to a nearby filling station after a friend told him a fuel tanker was on its way. He had gone several days without fuel.

Twelve people were already waiting when he arrived, but the situation soon turned chaotic.

“Minibus drivers and motorcycle taxi operators started arriving and jumping queues. They were so reckless they didn’t care if they bumped your vehicle. A scuffle erupted and I saw others, especially women, desperately trying to keep their place in the queue. It took me four hours to get 20 litres but others spent the night in the queue,” he told Al Jazeera.

The scramble for petrol has increasingly turned violent in Malawi’s cities and towns. Although the Malawi Energy Regulatory Authority publishes daily schedules indicating which filling stations are expected to receive fuel, motorists say uncertainty over deliveries makes it difficult to plan their journeys.

Videos of confrontations have circulated on social media, including footage appearing to show people attacking a man at a filling station. Al Jazeera could not independently verify the circumstances surrounding the incident.

The mayor of Blantyre has also been sued for assault following an incident at a fuel queue, while an attendant was killed after being struck by a vehicle during a commotion at a filling station, according to local media reports.

Purchases are reportedly rationed to 20 litres (5.3 gallons) a day, while motorists sometimes pay attendants for an additional five litres, Mhango said.

“The whole chaos that this has created is hectic. It is very hectic and it has created an atmosphere of uncertainty. This is happening when money is scarce, you have to make sure that you plan properly to survive,” he said.

On another occasion, Mhango arrived at Nyabadwe filling station in Blantyre at 5pm after joining a convoy of motorists searching for fuel. The tanker arrived at 9pm, and did not leave until 1am.

“My schedule has been completely altered. Now commuting is no longer a norm but a luxury. I have two parcels in town but I can’t even manage to go and get them,” he said.

Unable to find sufficient supplies at filling stations, Mhango turned to the black market. He paid 30,000 Malawian kwacha (about $17.31) for two litres of petrol for his father. On another occasion, he suspected fuel bought for his garage had been mixed with water after an engine malfunctioned.

“The crisis has completely changed and messed up everything. As a businessperson who deals with vehicles at my garage, people are no longer bringing their vehicles any more because of lack of fuel. And we can’t take our equipment to follow the client,” he said.

He added that his business was unlikely to meet its monthly targets, forcing him to consider docking the salaries of employees who assist him.

Selling fuel without the required permits is illegal in Malawi, but shortages have created opportunities for vendors to sell petrol at inflated prices.

Motorists who need to travel for work, business or medical care are increasingly turning to informal sellers despite the high prices and safety risks.

According to GlobalPetrolPrices, petrol in Malawi costs about $3.24 per litre, more than double the global average of approximately $1.52.

The informal trade has also proved deadly. Authorities have stepped up arrests of illegal vendors, while fires and explosions caused by unsafe fuel storage have killed people.

Earlier this year, petrol vendors and motorcycle taxi operators protested in Lilongwe after a suspected black market fuel seller was burned alive in an explosion following a police chase, local media reported.

Malawi’s Nation newspaper has documented at least six deaths from fuel explosions this year, including incidents involving families and children.

The shortages, alongside foreign-exchange problems and electricity blackouts, have fuelled demands for government accountability.

The Human Rights Defenders Coalition (HRDC) planned nationwide demonstrations on November 17, calling for the resignation of the energy minister over persistent fuel shortages and power cuts.

“We must therefore be clear that this is the responsibility of the government to ensure that fuel is normalised,” he said.

Twelve people were already waiting when he arrived, but the situation soon turned chaotic.

“Minibus drivers and motorcycle taxi operators started arriving and jumping queues. They were so reckless they didn’t care if they bumped your vehicle. news.originalContent:
The Salvadoran president has won popularity at home and abroad through a crime crackdown that has granted the state enormous power.

Salvadoran President Nayib Bukele is set to formally register his candidacy for his country’s upcoming presidential race, as he seeks a third consecutive term.

Thursday was the registration deadline for the election, which is slated for February 28, 2027.

The 45-year-old president has been widely expected to seek re-election, a move that would further consolidate his party’s leadership in the Central American country.

Bukele is the founder and leader of the Nuevas Ideas party, which controls El Salvador’s Legislative Assembly by a wide margin.

While El Salvador’s constitution previously prohibited presidents from seeking immediate re-election, the Supreme Court overturned that rule in 2021, paving the way for Bukele to run for a second term in 2024.

Then, in 2025, the Legislative Assembly passed a constitutional amendment allowing Bukele to seek a third term. The amendment also extended the length of a presidential term from five to six years.

Bukele secured his party’s nomination for the 2027 race in July. He is expected to return to the ballot alongside his current vice president, Felix Ulloa.

Bukele’s time in office has been defined by a crackdown on criminal gangs that has won him massive popularity at home and turned him into an icon for the political right across Latin America.

In 2022, his government announced a so-called state of emergency to address high levels of crime in the country.

It empowered the police to make sweeping arrests, but it also heralded the suspension of key civil liberties. Some people were detained without charge. Mass trials have been carried out, with hundreds of defendants being sentenced at a time.

More than 1 percent of the country’s population is estimated to have been arrested as a result, with little due process for those seeking to contest their guilt, according to human rights groups.

Advocates also warn that rights abuses, torture and poor conditions are systematic in Salvadoran prisons.

The state of emergency has been extended for years, although it was initially intended as a temporary measure and the government claims El Salvador’s gangs have been all but dismantled.

The United States Treasury has also accused Bukele’s government of negotiating with the gangs in secret, offering incentives to help lower crime.

But experts say human rights activists and members of the news media have seen their ability to monitor abuses and corruption in the country hampered under Bukele.

Some, like human rights lawyer Ruth Lopez, have allegedly been detained for their work without access to legal support. She has spent more than a year in “incommunicado detention”, according to the group Amnesty International.

Under Bukele, El Salvador has also passed a Foreign Agents Law that allows the government to restrict civil society groups that receive funding from abroad.

Those efforts have prompted allegations that Bukele has weaponised the state against his critics.

But those concerns have done little to dent his popularity, and Bukele is considered the clear favourite to win the election.

A handful of candidates, including Maytee Iraheta of the right-wing Nationalist Republican Alliance and Rafael Aguirre of the left-wing Farabundo Marti National Liberation Front, are also set to contest the presidency.

news.originalContent:
Four bodies have been recovered after a migrant boat capsized off Senegal’s coast, as authorities continue searching for survivors amid fears that the death toll could rise significantly.

Boubacar Seye, president of the nonprofit Horizons Sans Frontieres, confirmed the latest death toll to the Reuters news agency on Thursday, a day after the vessel capsized near the coastal town of Yenne, south of Dakar.

A local official said at least 50 people were aboard the boat, which struck a rock while migrants were being transferred from smaller fishing vessels to a larger wooden pirogue.

The number of people still missing remains unclear.

The incident comes amid an intensifying wave of attempted Atlantic crossings from West Africa to Spain’s Canary Islands, with migrant boats being intercepted or rescued almost daily.

New figures from Spain’s Interior Ministry show that 24,364 migrants reached the Canary Islands between January 1 and November 15, compared with 14,690 during the same period last year, an increase of nearly two-thirds.

The ministry had recorded just 13,327 arrivals by the end of October, meaning 11,037 people reached the archipelago in the first 15 days of November alone.

The surge has persisted despite extensive maritime operations. Senegal’s navy said it had rescued or intercepted 1,424 people on November 16 and 17, including passengers aboard nine fishing boats, according to the Senegalese Press Agency (APS).

Cheikh Sadibou Senghor, head of Senegal’s National Division for Combating Migrant Smuggling, said authorities had intercepted 6,889 people in operations linked to irregular migration, prevented 107 departures and dismantled 88 smuggling networks between January and November, APS reported.

Just days before the boat capsized, authorities announced the dismantling of a suspected migrant-smuggling network in Yenne itself, arresting 14 people and seizing two boats, three engines and 12.5 million CFA francs ($22,000), according to APS.

The United Nations refugee agency said nearly 600 people had died trying to reach the Canary Islands from West Africa so far this year, highlighting the dangers of the increasingly busy migration route.

As authorities struggle to contain the surge, Senegalese President Bassirou Diomaye Faye has called for greater efforts to improve employment opportunities for young people.

At a cabinet meeting on Wednesday, Faye requested a detailed assessment of the challenges facing efforts to curb irregular migration, according to a government statement cited by Reuters.

But Seye warned that tougher enforcement measures alone would not prevent further tragedies.

“We need to wake up to the gravity of the situation. The strategy deployed until now is not working,” he told Reuters.

“We need to fix the root causes of this problem.”

news.originalContent:
Tbilisi Mayor Kakha Kaladze said authorities would temporarily relocate 28 families.

Six people, including a child, have been killed after a suspected natural gas explosion caused part of a five-storey apartment building to collapse in Georgia’s capital, Tbilisi, according to the AFP news agency.

The blast struck the residential building in the suburban Ponichala district on Thursday morning, trapping several residents beneath the rubble.

Georgian Interior Minister Sulkhan Tamazashvili said rescuers had recovered six bodies from the wreckage, including that of a young child.

A three-year-old girl was pulled alive from the rubble after several hours of rescue operations, prompting applause from onlookers gathered at the scene.

Emergency Management Service chief Teimuraz Mgebrishvili said one of the women found dead was believed to be the girl’s mother, according to AFP.

Doctors at Ingorokva University Clinic said the rescued girl was in stable condition and scans had revealed no serious traumatic injuries, Georgian Public Broadcaster (1TV) reported.

An 11-year-old boy was also being treated in intensive care, although his condition was described as relatively stable, according to the broadcaster.

Tamazashvili said preliminary findings indicated that the explosion occurred on the fifth floor when a resident attempted to switch on a gas heater.

However, gas supplier Tbilisi Energy said the apartment identified as the likely source of the explosion had been registered as unoccupied and had recorded no gas consumption over the past year, according to 1TV. The company said it had not yet been able to inspect the damaged property.

Tbilisi Mayor Kakha Kaladze said authorities would temporarily relocate 28 families, comprising more than 100 residents, to hotels after structural assessments found two sections of the building unsafe, according to Georgia’s Interpressnews agency.

Prosecutor Levan Vepkhvadze said a criminal investigation had been launched into possible violations of safety regulations.

news.title: دیوان دادگستری بین‌المللی: میانمار علیه اقلیت روهینگیا مرتکب نسل‌کشی شده است
news.originalSummary:

این نخستین بار در تاریخ این دادگاه است که یک کشور برای نسل‌کشی مقصر شناخته می‌شود.

یوژی ایواساوا، قاضی دیوان، در جمع‌بندی اظهارات خود گفت میانمار قصد «نابود کردن» بخش قابل‌توجهی از جمعیت روهینگیا را داشته است.

او  افزود که میانمار به «نابودی گسترده شواهد» دست زده است و در تحقیق، پیگرد قضایی و مجازات افرادی که مرتکب  نسل‌کشی شده‌اند، کوتاهی کرده است.

قاضی ایواساوا در باره این پرونده همچنین گفت که مقیاس و ماهیت اقدامات میانمار و شیوه‌هایی که علیه این اقلیت به کار گرفته است «بسیار فراتر از آن چیزی بوده که برای مجازات این اقلیت لازم است و در عوض نشان‌دهنده قصد مقامات برای نابود کردن بخش قابل‌توجهی از این گروه است.»

آقای ماونگ اضافه کرد: «اظهارات قاضی بسیار دقیق و با جزئیات بود و تجربه‌ها و رنج‌هایی را که ما پشت سر گذاشته‌ایم منعکس می‌کند. اکنون نسبت به نتیجه این پرونده خوش‌بین هستیم و معتقدیم دادگاه نسل‌کشی علیه روهینگیا را به رسمیت خواهد شناخت.»

گزیده‌ای از مهم‌ترین خبرها، گزارش‌های میدانی و گفت‌وگوهای اختصاصی را هر هفته در ایمیل خود دریافت کنید.

این پرونده را ابتدا کشور گامبیا در دیوان دادگستری بین‌المللی علیه میانمار مطرح کرد اما میانمار آن را رد کرده و گفته بود که  نیروهایش در واکنش به حملات گروه‌های مسلح دست به عملیات زده‌اند.

میانمار همواره گفته است عملیات نظامی‌اش با هدف مقابله با تهدیدهای شبه‌نظامیان یا شورشیان انجام شده است.

کو کو هلائینگ، نماینده دولت میانمار، در ماه ژانویه به قضات دیوان دادگستری بین‌المللی  گفت کشورش «موظف نبود دست روی دست بگذارد و اجازه دهد تروریست‌ها در ایالت‌های شمالی راخین آزادانه فعالیت کنند.»

او تأکید کرد که عملیات ارتش با هدف «مقابله با شورش یا مبارزه با تروریسم»، در واکنش به حملات جنگجویان روهینگیا انجام شده بود.

روهینگیا اقلیتی قومی و مسلمان هستند که عمدتا در ایالت راخین میانمار زندگی می‌کنند.

آنها در میانمار، کشوری با اکثریت بودایی، دهه‌ها با تبعیض و خشونت روبه‌رو بوده‌اند و طبق قوانین این کشور از حق شهروندی محروم‌ هستند. در نتیجه، این اقلیت، از بزرگ‌ترین جمعیت‌های بدون تابعیت در جهان است.

موج‌های مختلف آزار و سرکوب در دهه‌های گذشته، از جمله عملیات گسترده نظامی در سال ۲۰۱۷، نزدیک به دو میلیون روهینگیا را مجبور به ترک کشور کرده است.

هر سال هزاران نفر همچنان از میانمار فرار می‌کنند؛ بسیاری از آنها با به جان خریدن سفرهای دریایی خطرناک و در قایق‌های بیش از حد شلوغ. سال گذشته یکی از مرگبارترین سال‌های اخیر برای پناهجویان روهینگیا بود و نزدیک به ۹۰۰ نفر از آنها در دریا جان باختند یا ناپدید شدند.

بیش از یک میلیون روهینگیای آواره در اردوگاه‌های پناهندگان در منطقه «کاکس بازار» بنگلادش زندگی می‌کنند. سازمان ملل آنها را «آزار‌دیده‌ترین اقلیت‌ در جهان» توصیف کرده است.

حکم تاریخی دیوان دادگستری بین‌المللی در مورد میانمار حالا می‌تواند به‌عنوان سابقه‌ای برای پرونده‌های دیگر در نظر گرفته شود از جمله پرونده‌ای که آفریقای جنوبی اسرائیل را به نسل‌کشی در غزه متهم کرده است. اسرائیل این ادعا را بی‌اساس خوانده است.

The 49ers received good news as they prepare to take on one of the NFL’s best defenses in the Vikings.

Star receiver Mike Evans returned to practice on Thursday for the first time since leaving the Oct. 19 game against the Commanders with Achilles tendinitis. San Francisco is practicing in Colorado Springs, Colo., to acclimate to the elevation ahead of Sunday’s game in Mexico City.

Getting Evans back could have big implications on the primetime game between the two teams vying for the NFC’s top seed. The Vikings (7-2) have the NFL’s second-ranked defense in yards allowed per game (273.3), and coordinator Brian Flores has typically given Kyle Shanahan fits over the years with his blitz-heavy scheme.

The 49ers have lost their last two games against the Vikings with Flores as defensive coordinator, scoring only 17 points in road losses in 2023 and 2024. Minnesota leads the NFL in quarterback pressure rate at 46.5% while blitzing on a league-high 72.3% of passing plays, according to Next Gen Stats.

WR Mike Evans (Achilles) is in uniform at 49ers’ practice and there is now looking like a decent chance he will be available to play Sunday night against the Vikings. pic.twitter.com/koigsscnjy

Evans had his biggest game of the season for San Francisco against the only defense that allows fewer yards than the Vikings when he caught seven passes for 113 yards and a touchdown during the Oct. 11 road win against the Seahawks. The future Hall of Famer leads the 49ers averaging 70 receiving yards per game.

Evans has been one of many 49ers wideouts to miss time with injury, yet Shanahan’s team has had one of the NFL’s best offenses throughout the season anyway. San Francisco put up a season-high 584 yards in Sunday’s win over the Cowboys in which Brock Purdy threw for 389 yards and three touchdowns.

Evans has missed three-plus games with the injury, while the 49ers have been without receivers Ricky Pearsall and rookie De’Zhaun Stribling for most of the season. Deebo Samuel just returned from a three-game absence with a hamstring injury, and Demarcus Robinson missed five games with a high ankle sprain.

The team’s injury situation led to San Francisco trading for former Colts receiver Keenan Allen ahead of the trade deadline. Allen had five catches for 61 yards in his 49ers debut against the Cowboys.

The 49ers have lost their last two games against the Vikings with Flores as defensive coordinator, scoring only 17 points in road losses in 2023 and 2024. Minnesota leads the NFL in quarterback pressure rate at 46.5% while blitzing on a league-high 72.3% of passing plays, according to Next Gen Stats.

WR Mike Evans (Achilles) is in uniform at 49ers’ practice and there is now looking like a decent chance he will be available to play Sunday night against the Vikings. pic.twitter.com/koigsscnjy

Evans had his biggest game of the season for San Francisco against the only defense that allows fewer yards than the Vikings when he caught seven passes for 113 yards and a touchdown during the Oct. 11 road win against the Seahawks. The future Hall of Famer leads the 49ers averaging 70 receiving yards per game.

Evans has been one of many 49ers wideouts to miss time with injury, yet Shanahan’s team has had one of the NFL’s best offenses throughout the season anyway. San Francisco put up a season-high 584 yards in Sunday’s win over the Cowboys in which Brock Purdy threw for 389 yards and three touchdowns.

Evans has missed three-plus games with the injury, while the 49ers have been without receivers Ricky Pearsall and rookie De’Zhaun Stribling for most of the season. Deebo Samuel just returned from a three-game absence with a hamstring injury, and Demarcus Robinson missed five games with a high ankle sprain.

The team’s injury situation led to San Francisco trading for former Colts receiver Keenan Allen ahead of the trade deadline. Allen had five catches for 61 yards in his 49ers debut against the Cowboys.

Christian Parker nearly took the easy way out of Dallas.

The Cowboys defensive coordinator had his play-calling responsibilities stripped given to defensive assistant Mike Pettine after a 46-40 loss to the 49ers last week,

Head coach Brian Schottenheimer admitted there were a lot of conversations going on this week, including one with Parker about leaving the Cowboys, ESPN NFL reporter Todd Archer reported Thursday.

However, Parker said “that would have been running from it.”

The 34-year-old called the situation a “significant” personal disappointment and said Pettine’s takeover is “only awkward if you make it that way.”

Against the 49ers, the Cowboys allowed 584 yards of offense — the most they have allowed at home in franchise history.

They were also completely fooled by coach Kyle Shanahan’s trick play in the third quarter that brought on a 70-yard touchdown from Deebo Samuel.

Schottenheimer called the defense “unacceptable” after the game and did not give Parker a vote of confidence.  Owner Jerry Jones didn’t have one for him either.

During an interview with 105.3 The Fan on Tuesday, the Jones was asked if the team was looking to make changes to Parker’s role.

“We’re talking about that, but I’m not going to talk about that here. But we are talking about those things,” Jones said.

Parker was a defensive backs coach in Denver and Philadelphia for five seasons before landing the gig in Dallas.

The Cowboys remain in the hunt for the playoffs at 4-6 due to a struggling NFC East. They sit three games behind Giants (5-3-1) in the loss column.

They will be hope Pettine can add some flavor to the defense. He previously served as the defensive coordinator for the Jets, Bills and Packers before taking on the Browns’ head coaching job from 2014-15.

Dallas hosts the 1-8 Titans next week followed by the 2-7 Eagles before visiting the defending Super Bowl champion Seahawks (6-4).

The franchise has missed the playoffs the past two seasons and has not made it to an NFC Championship game since winning the Super Bowl in 1996.

A Louisiana creep allegedly forced a young relative to do grueling 12-hour workouts and threatened to cut out his tongue — after the child told him he was gay, according to disturbing court documents.

Prince Daniel Cruz, of West Monroe, was arrested on Tuesday after a child reported abuse by a family member to the Louisiana Department of Children and Family Services.

The victim, who is not identified because of their age, said Cruz physically abused him after he came out to his relative, according to court documents seen by Louisiana First News.

Investigators claim Cruz, who found makeup and a pair of women’s underwear in the relative’s bedroom, flew into a rage and aggressively cut the child’s hair with clippers, leaving him with scrapes on his scalp.

“If you want to wear make-up like a clown, I will make you look like a clown,” Cruz allegedly told the child, before asking if he was ready to show everyone his “beautiful hair.”

Cruz also allegedly subjected the young victim to a grueling workout to physically punish him, forcing him to do 100 burpees, push-ups, sit-ups, and crunches.

Cruz told authorities he had been boxing with the victim and another child since the victim was 5 years old.

DCFS officials said the victim alleged that Cruz forced him and the other child into doing strenuous workouts that lasted for over 12 hours, stopping only for the bathroom and water.

Both children said they didn’t eat much, knowing Cruz would punch them in the stomach and make them vomit.

The court report also detailed a terrifying incident in which the victim described how Cruz allegedly once held a knife to his tongue and threatened to cut it off over a lie.

He also told investigators Cruz believes a spirit named “Jason” speaks to him, and that he claimed it was “Jason” who wanted the tongue, the docs state.

The child also stated that in 4th grade, Cruz whipped him and cut his hair after he forged his signature on a progress report. When a teacher reported it to DCFS, the child said Cruz punished him again.

news.originalContent:

New York City’s iconic Flatiron Building has officially gone from office landmark to home sweet home.

For the first time in its 124-year history, residents are moving into the famous triangular skyscraper at 175 Fifth Ave., following a highly anticipated transformation into ultra-luxury condominiums, The Post has learned.

And the building’s new residential chapter is already attracting big money.

Six apartments were marked sold on StreetEasy between late October and mid-November, with reported prices totaling approximately $118.6 million — nearly $120 million in just a matter of weeks.

Another 11 units are presently in contract, according to StreetEasy, with their combined listing prices totaling $234.5 million. Those deals have yet to close, and their final sale prices remain unknown.

City property records confirm at least one transaction: a residence that sold for $29.75 million on Oct. 28, according to a deed recorded with the Department of Finance on Nov. 18.

The first sales mark a major milestone for the Beaux-Arts landmark, which opened in 1902 and spent more than a century housing office workers rather than permanent residents.

The Brodsky Organization and Sorgente Group have transformed the building into 36 luxury residences, with interiors by acclaimed designer Studio Sofield.

Residents will have access to a 60-foot lap pool, a fitness center, a sauna, a cold plunge, a golf simulator and lounges overlooking Madison Square Park. The building also features a double-height attended lobby, while private wine cellars and storage units are available for purchase.

The ambitious restoration preserves the property’s historic architectural character while introducing contemporary residential interiors and amenities.

“We can now proudly say that for the first time in its storied history, The Flatiron Building is officially a residential address,” Dean Amro, principal at the Brodsky Organization, told The Post.

“It is especially rewarding to see our buyers share our enthusiasm for the building, and that they are so eager to call it home,” he added.

“As we put the finishing touches on this remarkable transformation, we are encouraged by the strong sales momentum and look forward to welcoming more residents while ensuring the Flatiron Building remains a cherished part of New York City for generations to come.”

Remaining three- and four-bedroom homes start at $14.85 million, while a 20th-floor residence is asking a staggering $53.5 million, according to the development’s latest marketing materials.

The latest milestone comes after a turbulent few years for one of Manhattan’s most recognizable buildings.

In March 2023, the Flatiron became the unlikely star of a dramatic court-ordered auction when investor Jacob Garlick placed a jaw-dropping $190 million winning bid. At the time, the building was the subject of a dispute among its co-owners, who didn’t know what to do with the longtime office property.

But the deal quickly unraveled after Garlick failed to produce the required $19 million deposit, forcing the property back onto the auction block.

Two months later, the owners secured the building with a $161.5 million bid.

The saga paved the way for an ambitious residential reinvention, turning a property once synonymous with Manhattan’s commercial history into one of the city’s most unusual luxury addresses.

The building’s first publicly listed apartment hit the market in January — an 11th-floor residence asking $16 million.

Demand quickly accelerated.

By April, nearly a dozen residences were already in contract, with combined asking prices exceeding $240 million, including a full-floor home listed for $58.5 million.

By August, the landmark was approaching a sellout, with 18 of 22 publicly marketed residences no longer available.

The building’s transformation is part of a broader wave of office-to-residential conversions across New York City, as developers seek new uses for aging commercial properties.

But few conversions come with the history, recognizable silhouette or price tags of the Flatiron.

news.originalContent:

Divisive sports broadcaster Dianna Russini quietly removed a photo of her husband and children from an Instagram post on Wednesday, after sharing the image alongside a strong declaration about the future of her career.

Hours after debuting the second episode of her new show on BetUS, Russini, 43, shared a new post on her social media account, featuring a carousel of three images, including a headshot and a snap of some flowers and cards seemingly sent to her in celebration of her latest venture.

In addition, she also included a photo of what appeared to be her bedside table, which was decorated with a framed wedding photo of herself and her husband, Shake Shack exec Kevin Goldschmidt, as well as another of their two children.

Also seen on the table was a note from her management company telling her to “f–king kill it.”

“Feeling loved. Feeling grateful. Back talking football, and I couldn’t do it without the best friends and family in the world. More to come…❤️,” Russini wrote in the caption of the post.

However, hours after sharing the post, Russini quietly removed the image showing the photos of her husband and her children, while leaving the other two intact.

It was not immediately clear what prompted Russini to remove the image; however, she notably limited the comments on the post.

Russini famously stepped down from her role at the New York Times’ The Athletic earlier this year following an investigation into her relationship with New England Patriots head coach Mike Vrabel.

Page Six has reached out to Russini’s reps for comment.

On Nov. 11, the NFL insider’s new show, “The Russini Report,” premiered on the online sportsbook platform, her first appearance since stepping down from the Times in April.

The show was slated to air live at 12 p.m. ET, but did not air until almost 1 p.m. ET due to an “overwhelming” number of viewers.

During the premiere, she subtly addressed the Vrabel controversy, noting that she’d had a “lot of time” to think about her priorities.

“Over the last few months, I have had a lot of time to think about my life and my priorities and the person I want to be moving forward and being home in New Jersey with my husband and our two little boys and being truly present,” Russini said at the top of the episode.

“It gave me so much perspective that I didn’t even know I needed.”

Russini went on to note that she also used her time away from the spotlight to figure out how to continue her career as an NFL insider, explaining that she’d spoken to several people in the industry — and outside it — to work out what her future might hold.

“I’ve also had a lot of long conversations with people all around football,” she said. “You know, some were about the game and others were just about life to the people who picked up the phone and checked in and offered both encouragement and honest advice, from the bottom of my heart, thank you.”

“Those conversations helped me find my way back to the work I love and back to myself, right here, hosting the show,” the journalist added.

The reporter’s return to the spotlight comes seven months after she resigned from her job at the New York Times’ The Athletic amid an investigation into her relationship with Vrabel.

The investigation was launched after Page Six published exclusive photos of the two cozying up together at an Arizona resort.

Page Six also obtained snaps of them kissing at Tribeca Tavern in New York City years before, in March 2020.

After Russini resigned, Vrabel was absent from Day 3 of the NFL Draft, having revealed that he was going to seek counseling.

The two deny any nefarious behavior, but The Athletic concluded at the end of the investigation that the two shared an inappropriate relationship.

The publication also stated that it “was in clear violation of The Athletic’s standards.”

The two remain married to their respective spouses. Russini has been married to Goldschmidt since 2020, while Vrabel has been married to his wife, Jen, since 1999.

news.originalContent:
With crowds rallying behind El Salvador’s deployment in Haiti, analysts question whether civilians are any safer.

The streets of Haiti’s capital, Port-au-Prince, rang out on Tuesday and Wednesday with chants from local residents in support of a president who was not their own: El Salvador’s Nayib Bukele. In a country where the scars of foreign intervention run deep, some Haitians are placing their hopes on another foreign force, this time from El Salvador, to help take their neighbourhoods back from armed gangs.

Thousands turned out to cheer on the roughly 2,500 soldiers Bukele has sent since October. What began as a narrow mission to rescue four missing Salvadoran aviation technicians has grown into a much broader military operation.

For some of those who marched, the intervention is exactly what the country needs after years of kidnappings, killings, and displacement, with little sign of relief.

But even with the Haitian government’s backing and a warm reception from the public, questions are growing about what the troops are doing on the ground and what kind of mark Bukele will ultimately leave on Haiti.

The immediate trigger came on October 18, when four Salvadoran aviation technicians working with the United Nations-backed Gang Suppression Force (GSF) went missing after armed men attacked their vehicle near Port-au-Prince.

The force was created to help Haitian authorities deal with a security crisis that has grown more severe since the 2021 assassination of President Jovenel Moise. According to Reuters, gangs now control more than 80 percent of the capital region, with Haitian and international forces struggling to reclaim that territory.

Shortly after the technicians went missing, Bukele announced a new military operation in Haiti, sending 100 special forces soldiers to rescue them. Since then, he’s sent about 2,500 in total.

Most of them are operating outside the UN-backed force and outside the UN support office’s monitoring mechanisms, according to UN spokesperson Stephane Dujarric.

And the deployment itself has turned from a narrow rescue operation to a broader offensive against Haiti’s gangs, with Salvadoran soldiers joining Haitian security forces, the GSF, and private contractors, including Blackwater founder Erik Prince’s Vectus Global.

Bukele, who gained international notoriety for a crackdown on gangs in El Salvador that led to a sharp decline in crime but has drawn widespread condemnation over human rights abuses, has been aggressively promoting the deployment on social media.

He has posted dramatic videos of helicopter attacks on gang leaders’ properties and, more recently, footage of rallies cheering on his troops.

“I never expected anything like this,” he wrote in a Tuesday post accompanying a video of a rally. “I hear you loud and clear. I love you, too.”

Neither the Haitian government nor the Salvadoran government replied to Al Jazeera’s requests for comment about the troops in Haiti.

The troops have landed amid a worsening humanitarian crisis in Haiti, with nearly 1.5 million people displaced from their homes, and violence making it difficult to access food and basic services. More than 22,000 people have been killed in gang-related violence, including security operations, since 2022, according to Reuters.

At rallies in Port-au-Prince and other parts of Haiti, demonstrators voiced support for the deployment. Some who spoke to The Associated Press news agency described losing loved ones to gang violence and being forced to leave their homes.

“The support we see from many Haitians comes from sheer desperation after years of failure and widespread terror,” Louimann Maceus, president of the human rights organisation Ensemble des Citoyens Competents a la Recherche de l’Egalite des Droits de l’Homme en Haiti (ECCREDHH), told Al Jazeera. “People are exhausted.”

“There is a genuine hope, especially among the hundreds of thousands of internally displaced people we work with who just want to return safely home,” said Maceus, who lives in Port-au-Prince.

That hope, he said, follows years of frustration with UN-backed forces, which he said had done little to improve security.

The Salvadoran deployment already outnumbers the GSF, according to numbers from the GSF’s special representative Jack Christofides, on October 18, when it had just surpassed 2,000 personnel.

International Crisis Group analyst Diego Da Rin also links some of the enthusiasm to what he describes as a really effective communication campaign by Bukele, whose videos of strikes on gang leaders’ homes are all over Haitian social media.

“These are symbolic wins that everybody was waiting for,” he said, adding that AI-generated videos were also circulating of gang leaders being arrested.

But support for the deployment is not universal. Da Rin pointed to the residents of gang-controlled areas.

“Many of these people, who clearly see the risks in these iron-fist operations, are extremely scared of being attacked and being collateral damage of any of these operations,” said Da Rin.

Security force clashes and drone strikes targeting gangs increased by 46 percent in the 21 days after the start of the deployment, compared to the 21 days before it, according to the conflict monitoring group the Armed Conflict Location & Event Data Project (ACLED).

ACLED estimated more than 100 people were killed in the same period, including at least 26 civilians.

Haiti’s Justice Minister Patrick Pelissier, however, said on Monday that the government had received no reports of civilian casualties in the latest operations, which it described as professional, according to Reuters.

Bukele has used social media to highlight what he sees as the offensive’s successes.

After Salvadoran troops joined Haitian police and a government task force in a November 8 attack on a house belonging to Wilson Joseph, leader of the powerful 400 Mawozo gang, Bukele posted video of helicopters repeatedly firing at the building, as people ran away from the area.

Joseph reportedly was not there and survived the attack.

A few days later, Haitian national police and Bukele announced that they’d retaken control of the national football stadium. Bukele shared video of robot dogs armed with rifles moving through the corridors of the stadium alongside troops, although it’s unclear how exactly they were used in the operation.

Da Rin said it was worth noting that police initially credited their officers and the task force with retaking the stadium before handing control over to Salvadoran troops, who set up a base there.

The stadium is a useful spot to launch operations against nearby gang strongholds, he added, but it represented a relatively small gain from positions Haitian forces had already secured.

On Wednesday, Bukele posted another video showing a helicopter attack on the home of Jeff Larose, leader of the Taliban gang, which controls the area of Canaan in northern Port-au-Prince.

It was not clear whether the attack had killed Larose or whether Haiti’s police or army had participated. The GSF was not involved, according to The Associated Press.

For displaced people looking to return home, the gains have yet to make a tangible difference, said Da Rin.

After the attack on Joseph’s house, none of the security forces set up a permanent presence in the area, he said.

With crowds rallying behind El Salvador’s deployment in Haiti, analysts question whether civilians are any safer.

The streets of Haiti’s capital, Port-au-Prince, rang out on Tuesday and Wednesday with chants from local residents in support of a president who was not their own: El Salvador’s Nayib Bukele. In a country where the scars of foreign intervention run deep, some Haitians are placing their hopes on another foreign force, this time from El Salvador, to help take their neighbourhoods back from armed gangs.

Thousands turned out to cheer on the roughly 2,500 soldiers Bukele has sent since October. What began as a narrow mission to rescue four missing Salvadoran aviation technicians has grown into a much broader military operation.

For some of those who marched, the intervention is exactly what the country needs after years of kidnappings, killings, and displacement, with little sign of relief.

But even with the Haitian government’s backing and a warm reception from the public, questions are growing about what the troops are doing on the ground and what kind of mark Bukele will ultimately leave on Haiti.

The immediate trigger came on October 18, when four Salvadoran aviation technicians working with the United Nations-backed Gang Suppression Force (GSF) went missing after armed men attacked their vehicle near Port-au-Prince.

The force was created to help Haitian authorities deal with a security crisis that has grown more severe since the 2021 assassination of President Jovenel Moise. According to Reuters, gangs now control more than 80 percent of the capital region, with Haitian and international forces struggling to reclaim that territory.

Shortly after the technicians went missing, Bukele announced a new military operation in Haiti, sending 100 special forces soldiers to rescue them. Since then, he’s sent about 2,500 in total.

Most of them are operating outside the UN-backed force and outside the UN support office’s monitoring mechanisms, according to UN spokesperson Stephane Dujarric.

And the deployment itself has turned from a narrow rescue operation to a broader offensive against Haiti’s gangs, with Salvadoran soldiers joining Haitian security forces, the GSF, and private contractors, including Blackwater founder Erik Prince’s Vectus Global.

Bukele, who gained international notoriety for a crackdown on gangs in El Salvador that led to a sharp decline in crime but has drawn widespread condemnation over human rights abuses, has been aggressively promoting the deployment on social media.

He has posted dramatic videos of helicopter attacks on gang leaders’ properties and, more recently, footage of rallies cheering on his troops.

“I never expected anything like this,” he wrote in a Tuesday post accompanying a video of a rally. “I hear you loud and clear. I love you, too.”

Neither the Haitian government nor the Salvadoran government replied to Al Jazeera’s requests for comment about the troops in Haiti.

The troops have landed amid a worsening humanitarian crisis in Haiti, with nearly 1.5 million people displaced from their homes, and violence making it difficult to access food and basic services. More than 22,000 people have been killed in gang-related violence, including security operations, since 2022, according to Reuters.

At rallies in Port-au-Prince and other parts of Haiti, demonstrators voiced support for the deployment. Some who spoke to The Associated Press news agency described losing loved ones to gang violence and being forced to leave their homes.

“The support we see from many Haitians comes from sheer desperation after years of failure and widespread terror,” Louimann Maceus, president of the human rights organisation Ensemble des Citoyens Competents a la Recherche de l’Egalite des Droits de l’Homme en Haiti (ECCREDHH), told Al Jazeera. “People are exhausted.”

“There is a genuine hope, especially among the hundreds of thousands of internally displaced people we work with who just want to return safely home,” said Maceus, who lives in Port-au-Prince.

That hope, he said, follows years of frustration with UN-backed forces, which he said had done little to improve security.

The Salvadoran deployment already outnumbers the GSF, according to numbers from the GSF’s special representative Jack Christofides, on October 18, when it had just surpassed 2,000 personnel.

“These are symbolic wins that everybody was waiting for,” he said, adding that AI-generated videos were also circulating of gang leaders being arrested.

But support for the deployment is not universal. Da Rin pointed to the residents of gang-controlled areas.

“Many of these people, who clearly see the risks in these iron-fist operations, are extremely scared of being attacked and being collateral damage of any of these operations,” said Da Rin.

Security force clashes and drone strikes targeting gangs increased by 46 percent in the 21 days after the start of the deployment, compared to the 21 days before it, according to the conflict monitoring group the Armed Conflict Location & Event Data Project (ACLED).

ACLED estimated more than 100 people were killed in the same period, including at least 26 civilians.

Bukele has used social media to highlight what he sees as the offensive’s successes.

Joseph reportedly was not there and survived the attack.

A few days later, Haitian national police and Bukele announced that they’d retaken control of the national football stadium. A three-way meeting between the leaders of China, Russia and the United States has yielded a number of commitments.

Xi Jinping hosted Vladimir Putin and Donald Trump in the city of Shenzhen, China on Thursday.

In a joint statement called a “Peace Declaration”, the three countries’ presidents pledged to safeguard international security and increase the production of refined petroleum products.

news.originalContent:
The lawsuit cited a book about Trump by two NYT reporters and what it said were ‘false, malicious, defamatory’ articles.

A federal judge has said United States President Donald Trump’s defamation lawsuit against The New York Times and book publisher Penguin Random House may proceed, a victory for Trump in his legal campaign against media companies he accuses of treating him unfairly.

US District Judge Steven Merryday, an appointee of former President George HW Bush, handed down the ruling in federal court in Tampa, Florida, on Thursday.

Trump has filed several lawsuits against media companies since 2024, alleging they defamed him or fraudulently misled the public with false coverage. His critics have denounced the lawsuits as attacks on the free press.

The lawsuit against The New York Times and Penguin Random House cited a book about Trump by two New York Times reporters and what it characterised as “false, malicious, defamatory, and disparaging” articles that he says were aimed at sabotaging his chances in the 2024 presidential election, which he won.

The Times and Penguin have denied defaming Trump and said in a court filing that his case is legally flawed and aimed at scoring political points.

Representatives for The New York Times, Penguin Random House and Trump’s personal lawyers did not immediately respond to requests for comment.

Merryday threw out two of Trump’s claims but said the rest of his complaint plausibly alleged that statements accusing Trump of “planning and perpetrating complex crimes” were “based on incomplete, minimal information”.

The lawsuit against The Times and Penguin concerned two articles and a book that cast doubts on his origin story as a savvy businessman who ascended in the real estate and entertainment industries.

Trump cited 22 statements from the book by Times journalist Peter Baker titled For Trump, a Lifetime of Scandals Heads Toward a Moment of Judgment, and 12 from the articles by Susanne Craig and Russ Buettner.

They include assertions about Trump’s role in creating his hit reality TV show The Apprentice, his inheritance from his father, his business ventures and upbringing in New York City.

The Times and Penguin said in a motion to dismiss that Trump’s lawsuit failed to explain how the statements were defamatory and included subjective opinions that cannot be proven true or false.

The latest victory comes days after another judge allowed Trump’s $10bn defamation lawsuit against the BBC to move forward. That civil case alleges that the British broadcaster deceptively edited a documentary on the January 6, 2021, riots on Capitol Hill to damage Trump’s reputation.

Trump, since resuming office last year, has undertaken a wider pressure campaign against the media and coverage he disagrees with. He has an ongoing $10bn lawsuit against The Wall Street Journal that he refiled in May after it had been dismissed. In September, he moved to bar CNN, MS Now and Politico from the White House and its press pool – a blanket ban a federal judge later blocked.

The US has fallen to a “historic low” in the Reporters Without Borders (RSF) annual press freedom tracker, continuing a decade-long decline, the organisation said earlier this year in its annual report.

While the US, during the first year of Trump’s second term, remained in the “problematic” category, it dropped seven places from 57th in the world to 64th.

In a statement, Clayton Weimers, executive director of RSF’s North America office, said at the time that the US was experiencing a “press freedom crisis”.

“Trump and his administration have carried out a coordinated war on press freedom since the day he took office, and we will live with the consequences for years to come,” he said.
