news.originalContent:
دونالد ترامپ و ولادیمیر پوتین پس از بیش از یک سال دیدار کردند درحالی‌که برای مذاکرات مهم و تاریخی در چین با حضور شی جین‌پینگ آماده می‌شوند.

رهبر چین از رئیس‌جمهور آمریکا هنگام ورود به شهر شنژن برای شرکت در نشست رهبران آسیا و اقیانوسیه (اپک) در پای هواپیما استقبال کرد.

دست دادن و در آغوش گرفتن دو رئیس‌جمهور در باند فرودگاه با دقت طراحی شده بود و از آقای ترامپ استقبال گرمی شد. رئیس‌جمهور آمریکا بعدتر در محل کنفرانس و مراسم خوشامدگویی رسمی به رهبران با آقای پوتین نیز دست داد و خوش‌وبش و تبادل تعارف کرد.

انتظار می‌رود دونالد ترامپ و ولادیمیر پوتین روز پنجشنبه در حاشیه این نشست، مذاکرات دوجانبه‌ای برگزار کنند که جنگ اوکراین از موضوعات گفت‌وگو است.

با این حال، تمرکز اصلی در جریان مجمع همکاری اقتصادی آسیا و اقیانوسیه، بر مذاکرات آمریکا، چین و روسیه در روز پنجشنبه خواهد بود؛ مذاکراتی که نخستین دیدار حضوری این سه رهبر محسوب می‌شود.

برنامه کامل مذاکرات هنوزمنتشر نشده اما اشاره‌های مختلفی به موضوعات احتمالی شده است از جمله جنگ‌های اوکراین و ایران، تسلیحات هسته‌ای، تنش‌های تجاری و تحولات حوزه هوش مصنوعی.

این نخستین دیدار حضوری آقای ترامپ و آقای پوتین از اوت ۲۰۲۵ بود که رهبر روسیه به آلاسکا سفر کرد اما مذاکراتش با رئیس‌جمهور آمریکا درباره جنگ اوکراین به جایی نرسید.

استقبال شخصی آقای شی از دونالد ترامپ در فرودگاه، اقدامی ویژه بود. در سفر قبلی اقای ترامپ به چین در ۲۳ اردیبهشت ۱۴۰۵، معاون آقای شی در فرودگاه به استقبال آقای ترامپ رفت. اما وقتی حدود چهار ماه بعد شی جین‌پینگ به آمریکا سفر کرد، آقای ترامپ در فرودگاه به استقبالش رفت.

این استقبال آقای شی اقدامی دیپلماتیک برای ایجاد فضایی دوستانه تلقی می‌شود.

گزیده‌ای از مهم‌ترین خبرها، گزارش‌های میدانی و گفت‌وگوهای اختصاصی را هر هفته در ایمیل خود دریافت کنید.

در شهر شنژن، برای استقبال از آقای ترامپ فرش قرمزی در مقابل هواپیمای ویژه ریاست‌جمهوری آمریکا (ایرفورس وان) پهن شده بود و جمعیتی از استقبال‌کنندگان، گارد تشریفات، عبور هواپیماهای نظامی از فراز محل و مراسم اهدای گل نیز برای خوشامدگویی به او تدارک دیده شده بود.

خبرگزاری دولتی شینهوا چین به نقل از آقای شی گزارش داد که او خواستار پیگیری «روابطی سازنده، راهبردی و باثبات، مبتنی بر احترام، انصاف و برابری» شده است.

شهر شنژن در جنوب شرقی چین که نشست اپک در آن برگزار می‌شود، منطقه‌ای پررونق صنعتی و فناوری‌های پیشرفته است.

این نشست در شرایطی برگزار می‌شود که جنسن هوانگ، مدیرعامل انویدیا، برکنار شده است درحالی‌که پذیرفت با زنی رابطه داشته که سازمان‌های اطلاعاتی آمریکا به جاسوسی برای پکن مظنون هستند. چین این را «افترا» خوانده و تکذیب کرده است.

ترامپ در پی بهبود روابط با چین بوده است، اما این رویداد نشان‌دهنده تداوم تنش‌ها میان این دو قدرت است.

چند ساعت پیش از ورود دونالد ترامپ، ولادیمیر پوتین وارد شنژن شد و حدود دو ساعت با شی جین‌پینگ گفت‌وگو کرد.

آقای شی پس از این دیدار گفت روابط دو کشور مثل «کوه» پابرجاست و باد و باران بر آن اثری نگذاشته است.

برنامه کامل مذاکرات هنوزمنتشر نشده اما اشاره‌های مختلفی به موضوعات احتمالی شده است از جمله جنگ‌های اوکراین و ایران، تسلیحات هسته‌ای، تنش‌های تجاری و تحولات حوزه هوش مصنوعی.

این نخستین دیدار حضوری آقای ترامپ و آقای پوتین از اوت ۲۰۲۵ بود که رهبر روسیه به آلاسکا سفر کرد اما مذاکراتش با رئیس‌جمهور آمریکا درباره جنگ اوکراین به جایی نرسید.

استقبال شخصی آقای شی از دونالد ترامپ در فرودگاه، اقدامی ویژه بود. در سفر قبلی اقای ترامپ به چین در ۲۳ اردیبهشت ۱۴۰۵، معاون آقای شی در فرودگاه به استقبال آقای ترامپ رفت. اما وقتی حدود چهار ماه بعد شی جین‌پینگ به آمریکا سفر کرد، آقای ترامپ در فرودگاه به استقبالش رفت.

این استقبال آقای شی اقدامی دیپلماتیک برای ایجاد فضایی دوستانه تلقی می‌شود.

گزیده‌ای از مهم‌ترین خبرها، گزارش‌های میدانی و گفت‌وگوهای اختصاصی را هر هفته در ایمیل خود دریافت کنید.

در شهر شنژن، برای استقبال از آقای ترامپ فرش قرمزی در مقابل هواپیمای ویژه ریاست‌جمهوری آمریکا (ایرفورس وان) پهن شده بود و جمعیتی از استقبال‌کنندگان، گارد تشریفات، عبور هواپیماهای نظامی از فراز محل و مراسم اهدای گل نیز برای خوشامدگویی به او تدارک دیده شده بود.

خبرگزاری دولتی شینهوا چین به نقل از آقای شی گزارش داد که او خواستار پیگیری «روابطی سازنده، راهبردی و باثبات، مبتنی بر احترام، انصاف و برابری» شده است.

شهر شنژن در جنوب شرقی چین که نشست اپک در آن برگزار می‌شود، منطقه‌ای پررونق صنعتی و فناوری‌های پیشرفته است.

این نشست در شرایطی برگزار می‌شود که جنسن هوانگ، مدیرعامل انویدیا، برکنار شده است درحالی‌که پذیرفت با زنی رابطه داشته که سازمان‌های اطلاعاتی آمریکا به جاسوسی برای پکن مظنون هستند. چین این را «افترا» خوانده و تکذیب کرده است.

ترامپ در پی بهبود روابط با چین بوده است، اما این رویداد نشان‌دهنده تداوم تنش‌ها میان این دو قدرت است.

چند ساعت پیش از ورود دونالد ترامپ، ولادیمیر پوتین وارد شنژن شد و حدود دو ساعت با شی جین‌پینگ گفت‌وگو کرد.

آقای شی پس از این دیدار گفت روابط دو کشور مثل «کوه» پابرجاست و باد و باران بر آن اثری نگذاشته است.

news.originalContent:
آصف مرچنت، مرد پاکستانی که به اتهام تلاش برای انجام اقدامات تروریستی و سازمان‌دهی طرح ترور با دریافت پول، به دستور سپاه پاسداران محکوم شده بود، با تعیین میزان مجازات، روز سه‌شنبه به ۲۷ سال و نیم زندان فدرال محکوم شد.

اهداف احتمالی طرحی که آصف مرچنت در ارتباط با آنها بازداشت شد شامل دونالد ترامپ، رئیس‌جمهور آمریکا، و جو بایدن، رئیس‌جمهور پیشین این کشور، بودند.

آصف مرچنت در ماه مارس، اندکی پس از آغاز جنگ ایران، در اتهام‌های تروریستی و توطئه برای قتل در ازای دریافت پول مجرم شناخته شد. او با مجازات حبس ابد روبه‌رو بود.

آصف مرچنت با دو اتهام روبه‌رو بود: تلاش برای ارتکاب اقدام تروریستی با ابعاد فراملی و توطئه برای قتل در ازای دریافت پول.

او در جریان محاکمه برای دفاع از خود شهادت داد و اعتراف کرد که یکی از اعضای سپاه پاسداران انقلاب اسلامی او را به خدمت گرفته بود.

مرچنت در شهادت خود گفت علاوه بر دونالد ترامپ و جو بایدن، نیکی هیلی، سفیر پیشین آمریکا در سازمان ملل متحد، نیز یکی از اهداف احتمالی این طرح ترور بوده است.

پس از کشته شدن قاسم سلیمانی آیت‌الله علی خامنه‌ای، رهبر وقت جمهوری اسلامی، در پیامی گفته بود «انتقام سختی» در انتظار کسانی خواهد بود که دست به این کار زده‌اند.

او پس از مراسم خاکسپاری قاسم سلیمانی هم تاکید کرده بود که «آمران» و کسانی که در کشته شدن او دخالت داشته‌اند نیز «باید انتقام پس دهند و این انتقام در هر زمانی که ممکن باشد، قطعی است.»

پنج سال پیش، علی القاصی مهر، دادستان وقت تهران، گفته بود که ۳۶ نفر از کسانی که به گفته او در کشتن آقای سلیمانی نقش داشته‌اند، ازجمله دونالد ترامپ، رئیس جمهور آمریکا شناسایی و برایشان حکم جلب صادر شده است.

او حتی گفته بود که درخواست جلب این افراد از طریق پلیس بین‌الملل هم پیگیری شده است؛ ا‌دعایی که پلیس بین‌الملل آن را رد کرد.

در آن زمان مقامات آمریکا این اظهارات دادستان تهران را «ترفند تبلیغاتی» ایران توصیف کردند و گفتند که هیچکس آن را جدی نمی‌گیرد.

قاسم سلیمانی، روز ۱۳ دی سال ۱۳۹۸ (۳ ژانویه، ۲۰۲۰) در حمله پهپادی نیروهای آمریکا در اطراف فرودگاه بغداد، هدف قرار گرفت و به همراه چند نفر دیگر، از جمله ابومهدی مهندس، فرمانده نیروهای حشد شعبی عراق، کشته شد.

Quentin Grimes lifted the Lakers with a big-name performance Tuesday night.

LA kicked off its four-game home stand with an overtime thriller against the Hornets and Grimes led the Lakers in scoring with a 47-point performance. The 26-year-old joined Kobe Bryant as the only players in Lakers franchise history with 10-plus three pointers made in a single game.

“It’s an honor to wear this jersey and be mentioned with a guy like that,” Grimes said.

There had been a lot of discourse surrounding the Lakers and the team’s ability to take the lead, but not maintain it throughout the game. Against Charlotte, a different tale was told.

“It’s an honor to wear this jersey and be mentioned with a guy like that."Quentin Grimes (47 PTS, 10 3PM) on joining Kobe Bryant as the only players in Lakers franchise history with 10+ 3PM in a single game 🤝Lakers rally back from 18 down to win their 9TH STRAIGHT GAME! pic.twitter.com/ribV7SklVa

The Lakers rallied back from an 18-point deficit to win their ninth straight game. It was a gutsy performance led by Grimes, who dominated the floor on a night where the team was shorthanded with both Austin Reaves and Walker Kessler out.

The game-tying three from Grimes to force overtime caused a loud uproar throughout Crypto.com Arena.

Luka Doncic also mustered 36 points, seven assists and six rebounds, despite struggling throughout the night on 13-of-34 shooting. But the Lakers remain in the win column thanks to a career-high performance by Grimes.

Entering Tuesday’s game, the guard was off to a slow start this season but evidently he was ready to put on a show when the Lakers needed him most.

British actor Noel Clarke appeared in a London court on Wednesday after being charged with sexual offenses against five women.

The “Star Trek Into Darkness” actor learned during the short hearing at Southwark Crown Court that his trial will begin next November, according to Sky News.

Clarke, 50, spoke only to confirm his name in court, the outlet reported.

Judge Tony Baumgartner confirmed the trial will tentatively last six to eight weeks, beginning on November 8, 2027. He also granted conditional bail for Clarke.

The “Doctor Who” actor has until his next court date, March 5, 2027, to submit an application to dismiss the charges. If he does, the Crown Prosecution Service and Clarke’s legal team will make their respective cases at a hearing in April, according to Variety.

Last month, Clarke pleaded not guilty to two charges of sexual assault, three charges of voyeurism and one charge of exposure. The alleged incidents involve five women and took place between 2007 and 2016.

Clarke was arrested at his London home in September 2025 and charged with the six sexual offenses a year later. He’s denied all allegations.

Shortly after Clarke was officially charged, actress Ruby Rose accused him of being a predator on the set of their 2021 thriller “SAS: Rise of the Black Swan.”

“Years ago he preyed on a woman who worked on our SAS film. I reported him. No one cared. I was told not to get involved. Nobody followed up. So many came forward, finally some justice,” Rose, 40, wrote on Threads in September.

Clarke was first accused of sexual misconduct by 20 women in an exposé published by The Guardian in 2021.

The allegations against the actor-producer included “sexual harassment, unwanted touching or groping, sexually inappropriate behavior and comments on set, professional misconduct, taking and sharing sexually explicit pictures and videos without consent, and bullying between 2004 and 2019,” the newspaper reported.

Clarke categorically denied every allegation The Guardian presented him with, only admitting that he once made inappropriate comments about one accuser, for which he said he later apologized.

The “Adulthood” star also told the Associated Press at the time that he was “seeking professional help.”

“I vehemently deny any sexual misconduct or criminal wrongdoing. Recent reports however have made it clear to me that some of my actions have affected people in ways I did not intend or realize. To those individuals, I am deeply sorry. I will be seeking professional help to educate myself and change for the better,” he said in a statement.

Clarke later sued The Guardian for the exposé, but he lost the libel case in August 2025 and was forced to pay £3 million ($4 million) of the newspaper’s legal costs.

Clarke is the third British star to be in the headlines recently for sexual assault allegations.

Comedian and actor David Walliams, 55, was accused by a slew of women of grooming them for sex as young women, when some were as young as 15.

The bestselling children’s book author issued a denial — but did share his “regret” over “behav[ing] thoughtlessly towards other people [he] had casual sexual relationships with” in the past.

Before the accusations were made public, Walliams’ attorney claimed the ex-“Britain’s Got Talent” judge was “highly likely” to die by suicide if the allegations came to light.

Meanwhile, Russell Brand, 51, was found guilty of rape and sexual assault on Nov. 4 following a nearly four-week trial, and was sentenced to more than 10 years in prison.

The “Rock of Ages” star’s conviction stems from incidents in the 2000s.

The disgraced comedian is currently locked up at HMP Littlehey, which reportedly holds an estimated 1,200 male sexual offenders.

news.originalContent:
See more of our coverage in your search results.

Alabama quarterback Keelon Russell’s mom, April Moore, filed a wrongful death lawsuit on June 15 over the death of his twin sister, Kierston, last summer, the Tuscaloosa News reported Tuesday.

Kierston, 18, reportedly was experiencing ongoing abdominal discomfort and irregularities in sleep and eating habits before being found unresponsive June 3 at the AC Hotel in Tuscaloosa, Ala. and was declared dead after being rushed to a local hospital.

Moore’s lawsuit, which demands a jury trial, points to the hotel and Marriott International as liable for not appropriately responding to an emergency call and for a lack of proactive care, more specifically the lack of a working Automated External Defibrillator (AED), per the Tuscaloosa News.

The defense reportedly has since denied these claims and added there is no evidence to support that the hotel and its staff failed to act in the state of emergency.

Per the defense, Moore found her daughter unresponsive in the hotel room’s bathroom and called 911 at 9:55 p.m. CT and started to administer CPR, according to the report.

A hotel employee reportedly later arrived at the room. Moore claims they did not have an AED handy nor did they come in the room or offer help.

EMS later arrived and confirmed Kierston’s cardiac arrest and began treatment.

“The hotel never, ever, ever brings an AED, which my experts say would have saved Kierston at that point. This being a ‘fancy hotel,’ this being a hotel under the Marriott brand, you would expect that certain hotels have the proper equipment, emergency or otherwise, to take care of its guests,” Derrick Mills, who represents Moore, said to the outlet. “… Not only did they not have an AED, they weren’t trained on proper CPR, and they literally frustrated April’s efforts in trying to revive her daughter.

“So, you imagine trying to save your daughter or save your loved one, and in addition to not having the proper equipment, the hotel frustrates those efforts by interrupting April as she’s trying to perform life-saving measures.”

The hotel claimed they did not receive a call from an emergency dispatcher at the time. Rather, they heard of the incident from another guest, who reported hearing screaming from Moore’s hotel room, according to the Tuscaloosa News.

They reportedly additionally cited that the 911 call recording confirms that Moore did not stop performing CPR to open the hotel door, and three minutes elapsed between the time the hotel employee, who brought a master key, entered the room and EMTs began treating Kierston.

Rebecca Young, who represents the defense, declined to comment to The Tuscaloosa News, as it’s a “pending case.”

In her lawsuit, Moore reportedly is aiming to hold any employers, management companies and others that hired, trained or managed the employees involved responsible.

Keelon, a sophomore, has thrown 2,480 yards for 21 touchdowns and six interceptions for the 8-2 Crimson Tide, who are third in the latest College Football Playoff rankings.

The quarterback has his sister mentioned in his Instagram bio: “KIERSTON MCKENZIE RUSSELL💕🫶🏾🕊️”

The two graduated from Duncanville High School (Texas) together last May.

Kierston, who played basketball in high school, was set to join her brother at Alabama last August, ESPN previously reported.

news.originalContent:

A 25-year-old influencer with more than 3 million followers online died three years after she announced she had been diagnosed with cancer, her devastated family announced.

Catalina Fernández, a Colombian content creator known on social media as Cata Amatista, died Thursday last week after her long battle with brain cancer, a journey she shared with her heartbroken followers, People magazine reported.

“Cata was — and will always be — an extraordinary being of light. She was a child full of love, life, joy, and dreams, possessing a beautiful gift for finding magic in the smallest of things,” her family wrote in a touching tribute on her Instagram.

“Until her very last moment, she taught us how to live, to be grateful, to enjoy life, to offer tight embraces, and to understand that life is a gift worth celebrating every single day.”

The drama student first shared that she had cancer in a July 2023 YouTube video in which she said her bad headaches turned out to be from cerebellar medulloblastoma, a fast-growing tumor that originates in part of the brain.

She shared with her followers her difficulties over the next three years going through treatments, including surgeries and chemotherapy, Spanish-language news outlet Clarin reported.

The drama student garnered over 3 million followers across Instagram, YouTube and TikTok.

“If there is one thing we want you to take away from Cata, it is this: cancer was not her whole story. Her story was love — the way she chose to live, the joy with which she embraced each day, and the light she shared even when the path became difficult,” her family said in the Instagram post, which has received more than 1.3 million likes.

“We choose to remember her not through her absence, but through everything she gave us; for there are some people who do not need to remain physically present to stay with us forever.”

Fernández’s friends and fans flooded the comments.

“Cata will always be remembered for the light so beautiful she carried inside, because her energy was always powerful and magnetic,” said fellow influencer Zamu.

“Cata is and will always be an example of struggle, consistency and strength. We will always remember her with her beautiful smile and the positivity she spread to all of us,” influencer Camilo Triana wrote.

Florence Pugh is hitting back at the haters and speculators.

After Evie Magazine posted a breakdown of her supposed facial transformation, Pugh herself shut down the plastic surgery rumor.

“Guys. I turned 30. I’m a woman. Body’s and faces change,” she wrote. “It’s not that deep, the fact that people can’t even tell between what’s aging and what’s surgery is disturbing.”

Continuing, “Sadly puppy fluff doesn’t last forever ❤️.”

“I think that we can all collectively agree that Hollywood seems to have this thing against softer features,” the video began.

Calling “this sculpted, snatched look” the “most desirable” look in the modeling and celebrity world right now.

The speaker pointed to Pugh’s “more defined” and “more sharp” jaw as well as “pointier” chin as evidence that she has had work done.

“I just think she is naturally beautiful” the speaker shares of Pugh, adding, “I don’t think we should be demonizing celebrities for potentially getting plastic surgery … they’re just victims of these beauty standards.”

Pugh’s comment sparked lots of replies praising her.

“@florencepugh oh I LOVE you,” wrote one, while another added, “can we stop normalizing discussing women’s bodies? At the end of the day it doesn’t change your life or impacts it.”

news.originalContent:

The Cowboys’ saga on defense continues.

After days of speculation, ESPN reported Wednesday that defensive coordinator Christian Parker will remain in his position, but senior defensive coordinator Mike Pettine will instead call defensive plays during games.

The update comes after head coach Brian Schottenheimer hesitated to give Parker a vote of confidence and ripped his defense following a 46-40 home loss to the 49ers on Sunday.

“At the end of the day, the tackling and some of the covered stuff really led to the [explosive plays],” Schottenheimer said. “I’m taking a deep dive and looking at everything.”

Cowboys owner Jerry Jones added to the speculation when he said during a radio appearance Tuesday that Parker’s position has come up in conversations, but did not give further detail.

“We’re talking about that, but I’m not going to talk about it here,” Jones said on 105.3 The Fan. “But we are talking about those things.”

The Cowboys allowed 584 total yards Sunday, the most they’ve allowed in a home game in franchise history.

They’re now ranked as the worst defense in the NFL, allowing 393.8 yards per game and 33 total touchdowns, a mark that only trails the Raiders and Cardinals.

Parker, 34, is the youngest defensive coordinator in team history and is in his first coordinator role of his career.

He spent the 2024 and 2025 seasons as Philadelphia’s defensive passing game coordinator and saw success working with Quinyon Mitchell and Cooper DeJean, as well as Patrick Surtain II from his time in Denver.

Pettine served as the Browns’ head coach from 2014-15, and was previously the defensive coordinator for the Jets, Bills and Packers.

news.originalContent:
Cal-Maine reports avian influenza at Florida site, with 2.7 percent of its total flock affected.

Cal-Maine Foods, the largest egg producer in the United States, has said it would cull 1.8 million birds after avian influenza was detected at one of its facilities in Florida.

On Wednesday, the company said the 1.4 million laying hens and 360,000 young hens being culled account for 2.7 percent of its flock. Production at the facility will be temporarily halted.

Cal-Maine said in a statement that it would coordinate with other production and distribution facilities to minimise disruption across the company.

The risk bird flu poses to human health is low. According to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), there have been 74 human cases since February 2024, with no evidence of human-to-human transmission.

However, the virus continues to pose a significant challenge to the US poultry and egg industries. Some 21.5 million birds have been affected this year, following a historic surge in outbreaks in late 2024 and early 2025 that sharply reduced the number of egg-laying hens.

Approximately 50.7 million laying hens were lost between mid-October 2024 and early March 2025, when egg prices in the US reached a record high of $6.23 per dozen.

The current average retail price of eggs is $2.32 per dozen, according to the Bureau of Labor Statistics.

Despite the announcement that production at the Florida facility would be temporarily halted, Cal-Maine’s stock rose 5.3 percent in early trading.

news.originalContent:
Behind promises of jobs and investment lie threats to ancestral lands, water security and national sovereignty.

The Philippine government is promising jobs and billions in investment through the United States-led Pax Silica initiative. But protesters see a very different future: threatened ancestral lands, environmental destruction and deeper dependence on Washington.

On November 15, ahead of Donald Trump’s visit to Manila for the ASEAN summit, Philippine police arrested more than 200 demonstrators opposing the initiative. The arrests were part of a wider crackdown on protests against a project that critics see as another form of US neo-imperialism.

The Pax Silica initiative is a US-led coalition aimed at securing supply chains and countering China’s strength in critical minerals, semiconductors and other technologies essential to AI infrastructure. The Philippines joined the initiative in April 2026, with a proposed industrial hub in New Clark City, Tarlac province, forming part of it. The Philippine government has promoted the proposed industrial hub as essential to economic development, projecting that it could generate more than 130,000 jobs and attract up to $70bn in investment once fully developed, a process expected to take decades. The proposed Pax Silica industrial hub, which covers approximately 1,618 hectares, raises concerns not only about national sovereignty but also about the displacement of local communities, environmental repercussions, Indigenous land rights and human security.

Critics see the project as taking land from local communities and farmers to serve foreign interests. The Aeta Hungey community in Sapang Kawayan, for example, faces relocation from land it has occupied for generations. Around 200 residents could lose access to their homes, farmland, water sources and burial grounds, while the community’s efforts to secure formal recognition of its ancestral land, dating back to 1994, remain unresolved.

Another major concern is water consumption. According to the Bases Conversion and Development Authority (BCDA), the proposed industrial hub could require 65–90 million litres of water daily. Although the BCDA plans to meet this demand through surface-water harvesting, concerns remain about the pressure on water resources, particularly during droughts. The Philippines is already vulnerable to drought, water shortages, agricultural disruption and climate change. On November 4, the Philippine Atmospheric, Geophysical and Astronomical Services Administration (PAGASA) confirmed that a very strong El Nino was present and expected to persist into the first half of 2027.

The Philippine government must respond to the pressing needs of Filipinos instead of becoming a pawn of the United States in its geopolitical rivalry with China. Southeast Asia is a focal point of competition between the two major powers, with the Philippines serving as a key US ally. Pax Silica would position the Philippines as a central node in an emerging AI Cold War with China.

Projected as an avenue for economic progress, Pax Silica could also serve as a tool for the military expansion of the US in the region, particularly in the Philippines. Semiconductors are used in modern military production and are essential components of weapon systems in modern warfare. During his November 17 ASEAN speech, Trump highlighted US agreements across the region involving critical minerals, energy and technology, while describing the Philippines as a longstanding key ally. He also pointed to increased defence cooperation between the two countries. This cooperation already rests in part on the Enhanced Defense Cooperation Agreement (EDCA), which allows US forces access to agreed Philippine military facilities.

President Ferdinand Marcos Jr also emphasised the depth of the relationship between the two countries, rooted in shared history and values. Describing the extent of US influence in Philippine life, he said, “There is no part of our lives in the Philippines that is not involved with the United States in some way, in some shape or form or another.”

An unexamined alliance compromises national interests, particularly those affecting the lives of the Filipino people. Economic development should not come at the expense of human security, sovereignty and environmental sustainability.

Against this backdrop, a broad, multisectoral opposition movement against Pax Silica has emerged and is gaining momentum. It brings together diverse sectors, including Indigenous peoples, farmers, workers, scientists, environmentalists, faith leaders, students, and progressive activists.

The protests have also spread to university campuses. On November 13, university students staged coordinated campus walkouts across the Philippines. Among the major participating universities were the University of the Philippines, De La Salle University, Ateneo de Manila University, University of Santo Tomas, and Far Eastern University, among others. United in their opposition to Pax Silica, protesters repeatedly chanted slogans denouncing US imperialism. Drawing on the Philippines’ history as a former US colony, they associate the initiative with another neocolonial project by an imperial power.

In the Bangsamoro Autonomous Region in Mindanao, where anti-Pax Silica demonstrations took place in Marawi City and Tawi-Tawi, the opposition is particularly significant. For protesters in this predominantly Muslim region, opposition to the initiative intersects with longstanding grievances rooted in the historical dispossession of local communities whose ancestral lands were taken by settlers, reinforced by imperialist wars and oppression. They see Pax Silica as another project that could displace local communities and facilitate land-grabbing by an imperial power.

Equally important is the movement’s expansion beyond the Philippines into transnational solidarity. According to organisers, solidarity demonstrations have taken place in 23 cities across 14 countries, bringing international support to the opposition against Pax Silica and US imperialism.

As the movement gains momentum, the Marcos administration must address the legitimate grievances of the people directly affected by the proposed project. Moreover, this is not merely a concern of the Indigenous Aeta communities; it carries broader regional implications. Marcos’s reference to shared history does not necessarily mean that the two countries stand on equal footing. There is no symmetrical relationship between a coloniser and a colonised. Those subjected to imperial domination are not equal to those imposing control.

The ASEAN Way, characterised by the principle of consensus, must prevail over the competing interests of major powers. Fostering multilateralism will pave the way for cooperation, collective security and economic progress that will eventually empower ASEAN and the Global South. It is through this approach that the three major priorities of the Philippine ASEAN chairship can be realised: Peace and Security Anchors, Prosperity Corridors, and People Empowerment.

The views expressed in this article are the author’s own and do not necessarily reflect Al Jazeera’s editorial stance.

news.originalContent:
In an unprecedented move, Chinese President Xi Jinping welcomed President Donald Trump at an airport in Shenzhen, China, on Wednesday.

Video of the presidents’ reunion shows Xi standing on the tarmac, accompanied by a welcoming crowd, as he waited for Trump to descend from Air Force One. (RELATED: China Caught Copying American AI’s Homework, Hundreds Of Documents Show)

The two leaders shook hands before embracing, with Trump appearing to say something to Xi before patting him on the back.

A young girl then approached the world leaders and offered Trump a bouquet of flowers as the crowd cheered and waved American and Chinese flags. Trump greeted several more people before the crowd quieted and the national anthem began to play.

Trump’s current trip to China marks his first return since a historic state visit in May. He is expected to join Xi at an Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation banquet Wednesday before meeting with Russian President Vladimir Putin on Thursday.

Xi personally greeted Trump at the airport to return a similar gesture Trump offered when the Chinese president landed at Joint Base Andrews in Maryland, in September, according to CNN,

During the visit, both Trump and Xi emphasized the importance of stronger relations between the two nations as they struck deals involving trade and artificial intelligence.

Chinese President Xi Jinping welcomes US President Donald Trump upon his arrival at Shenzhen Bao’an International Airport to attend the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) Summit in Shenzhen, in China’s southern Guangdong Province on November 18, 2026. (Photo by Mark Schiefelbein / POOL / AFP)

The leaders’ warm greeting comes as Trump’s administration grapples with a scandal involving Jensen Huang, the now-former CEO of America’s largest chip manufacturing company, Nvidia. Huang has been accused of cheating on his wife with a Chinese asset who allegedly shipped more than $7.5 billion worth of Nvidia chips to Chinese technology firms over the last three years.

The location of the meeting also carries significance. Shenzhen serves as the base for several Chinese technology giants, including Huawei, Tencent, DJI, and BYD, now the world’s largest electric vehicle maker, NBC reported.

news.originalContent:
The New York congressman was nominated after Democrats gained control of Congress in the midterm elections.

Washington, DC, USA – Hakeem Jeffries has become the first Black lawmaker officially nominated for Speaker of the United States’ House of Representatives, marking a milestone in the country’s political history.

In a closed-door vote in Washington, DC, on Wednesday, the 56-year-old New York congressman secured his party’s nomination, just weeks after Democrats scored sweeping victories in the midterm elections, reclaiming control of both chambers of the US Congress.

Before the vote, Jeffries confirmed plans to force members of his party to take a recorded vote amid growing dissent among progressives over his leadership.

Some of those members, most of whom were newly elected earlier this month, declined to say whether they would support Jeffries, with several saying they wanted a leader who would support bold, populist policies they had campaigned on.

One of the most vocal holdouts, Congressman-elect Don Leonard of Ohio, refused to commit to Jeffries unless he received guarantees on some progressive priorities, including halting US military aid to Israel and reforming campaign finance standards set by the Supreme Court case Citizens United.

“Unless Speaker Jeffries is willing to commit to enforcing our nation’s laws like the Leahy Law against Israeli genocide in Gaza, unless the speaker is willing to get to the heart of this crisis, which is Citizens United, he will not have my vote,” the Ohio Democrat said in a video posted to social media.

Jeffries has received pushback within some Democratic circles over his record on Israel and ties to pro-Israel lobbying groups, like AIPAC. During an interview with The Atlantic on Tuesday, the Democratic lawmaker addressed some of that criticism, calling for “dramatic change” in the Middle East and a two-state solution.

Despite some opposition in Wednesday’s vote, Jeffries received overwhelming support from the US House Democratic Caucus, with 251 members voting to back his candidacy. Only 11 members opposed.

Just before Wednesday’s vote, Jeffries took to social media to post a Bible verse from the book of Corinthians reading,” For we walk by faith, not by sight”.

In 2023, Jeffries was put forward by Democrats as their pick to succeed former US House Speaker Kevin McCarthy, who was ousted by his fellow Republicans in favour of the chamber’s current speaker, Mike Johnson. Wednesday’s vote, however, means Jeffries has now been formally nominated by members of his party.

Jeffries is now poised to replace Johnson as speaker when the new Congress is sworn in on January 3.

news.originalContent:
Most of the casualties were in strikes on Odesa that President Volodymyr Zelenskyy described as ‘brutal’.

Russian air attacks across Ukraine have killed at least five people, authorities said, a day after a Ukrainian strike on Russia’s Kerch Bridge killed two and caused part of the structure to collapse.

In the southern city of Odesa, at least four people were killed and 13 others wounded in Russian air strikes, with President Volodymyr Zelenskyy saying the “brutal and deliberate” attack also targeted first responders.

Oleg Kiper, the head of the Odesa region’s military administration, said three Russian strikes hit the city’s “historic centre”. Odesa city council said one of the strikes hit a UNESCO-protected area, causing a car to catch fire and blowing out hundreds of windows in at least seven buildings.

Ukrainian emergency services shared images showing wounded people on stretchers, buildings with shattered windows and firefighters extinguishing a blaze on a rooftop.

“There were double-tap strikes after first responders and police officers had already arrived at the scene,” Zelenskyy wrote on X.

He said the attack served as “further proof of what the Russians really want and how they truly regard diplomatic efforts”.

In the southeastern Zaporizhia region, a Russian drone strike killed a woman and injured a man in the town of Kushuhum, local military administration official Mykhailo Semykin said.

Attacks on the region also forced local authorities to order families with children to leave the village of Balabyne, he said.

“We are talking about 85 children from 80 families. In total, the evacuation affects 184 people,” he wrote on Telegram.

In northern Ukraine’s Rivne region, 80 settlements were left without electricity after a Russian attack, authorities said. No deaths or injuries were reported.

Ukraine’s Energy Ministry says Russia has launched more than 1,000 attacks on energy infrastructure since September. New power outages had been recorded in Dnipropetrovsk, Donetsk, Zhytomyr, Zaporizhia, Kharkiv, Sumy, Rivne, and Cherkasy regions in the last 24 hours, Interfax reported on Wednesday. Russia has increased attacks on Ukraine’s energy infrastructure in the lead-up to winter, in a strategy the United Nations said amounted to war crimes.

“The situation in the Dnipropetrovsk and Kharkiv regions remains extremely difficult. Energy workers are doing everything possible to restore power supply as soon as possible, but repeated attacks are significantly complicating repair work,” Ukraine’s energy ministry said.

The attacks came a day after Ukraine attacked Russia’s Kerch Bridge – a symbolic road-and-rail link from Russia to the annexed Crimean peninsula – killing two people.

As the warring sides continue to trade long-range attacks, the European Commission has proposed a new 45 billion euro ($49.5bn) loan to Ukraine to help fill a 70 billion euro ($76.8bn) funding gap for next year.

European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said Ukraine would only need to repay the loan after Russia had paid reparations for damage caused since it launched its full-scale invasion in February 2022.

“We very much hope for the swift adoption of this decision by the European Parliament and the Council and count on the support of all EU member states,” Zelenskyy wrote on X.

Below is State of the Day, a morning newsletter from the Daily Caller Editorial Desk. Sign up here.__________

Welcome to State of the Day,

Your tax dollars are funding a War Department that can’t account for its own finances

The Pentagon Failed Another Audit. Now It Wants More Money

Most of us wouldn’t keep writing checks to someone who can’t explain where the last one went.

Nevertheless, Washington has no such reservations when it comes to the Pentagon.

Nine years ago, the Defense Department began undergoing financial audits — and it has yet to pass one.

But first, what exactly is an audit? Essentially, it’s a full financial shakedown of any given organization. Auditors review records to see whether they match what the company owns, owes, and how it spends its money.

They’ll look through transactions, liabilities, assets, and the systems in place to track them. The goal of an audit is to ensure the financial claims being made by the organization or department in question are accurate and can be substantiated.

In the Pentagon’s case, it’s been an unfulfilled goal for nearly a decade, and it’ll be another year before they get another chance to pass.

But that isn’t stopping the money-hungry Pentagon brass from asking for more of our tax dollars.

The DOW’s official funding request for the next fiscal year runs the tab to a historic 1.45 trillion dollars. On top of that, the Administration has also asked for $350 billion in additional mandatory funding through reconciliation, in part to replace munitions lost in the Iran War.

If you’re wondering why the world’s most technologically advanced military can’t pass a financial audit — you’re not alone — I am similarly at a loss.

In true government fashion, the failures can largely be attributed to a bloated bureaucracy. The Pentagon runs nearly 150 unique financial systems.

Some of these systems rely on code that is roughly half a century old. That’s right: the financial infrastructure underpinning the world’s most powerful military runs on technology that predates the fall of the Soviet Union.

Yet despite its technological limitations, the War Department’s limit on the tax dollars it’s willing to spend doesn’t seem to exist.

The 1.45 trillion-buck request comes in at forty-four percent more than the chunk of change Congress kicked across the river last year.

I might be going out on a limb here, but maybe just maybe, we could spend American tax dollars on actually helping Americans for once?

I know it sounds silly, but it is our money at the end of the day. And I, for one, don’t care to see any more of my paycheck going overseas to carpet bomb Palestinian children or, for that matter, into the greedy hands of defense contractors.

But Washington seems to give less than a damn about what we want — their motivations do carry the moral high ground, after all. If you’ve any doubt, just take a look at the stunning, recently unveiled Lockheed Martin Senator Lindsey Graham Welcome Center.

Who would choose affordable living, cheap gas, the ability to feed your family, or owning a home over getting your very own LOCKHEED MARTIN WELCOME CENTER!

I joke, of course — but that is the mentality that has taken hold of the federal lawmakers who will inevitably approve a check for the Pentagon of magnitudes larger than they should get.

And that psyche is really the problem here.

The folks responsible for appropriating these massive sums of our money are the same people who’ve spent much of their professional lives cultivating relationships with the defense industry — the people whose profits directly correlate with the size of the Pentagon’s budget any given year.

The kickbacks they’re getting are no chump change either.

An analysis of federal campaign finance filings connected more than $1.29 million in defense-industry money during the 2026 election cycle to the four lawmakers who lead the House and Senate Appropriations defense subcommittees.

Reps. Ken Calvert of California, Betty McCollum of Minnesota, and Sens. Chris Coons of Connecticut, and none other than Mitch McConnell of Kentucky.

That’s four members of Congress making an average of over a quarter of a million dollars from the defense sector alone, and they’re the four members with the most influence over how much money the Pentagon gets.

Meanwhile, the Pentagon can’t balance its checkbook, and we’re still endlessly asked to keep sending more and more of our money to the DOW.

Before Congress hands the Pentagon another blank check to spend without accountability, Americans ought to demand answers and explanations for the last nine checks that’ve already hit the bank.

news.originalContent:
Tensions surge between PM al-Zaidi’s government and Kataib Hezbollah amid oil-smuggling scandal.

Jurf al-Sakhar, a stronghold of Iran-linked fighters in Iraq, has emerged as the focal point of a sweeping anticorruption campaign launched by Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi’s government following accusations of oil smuggling.

Located some 60km (37 miles) southwest of Baghdad and spanning roughly 345 square kilometres (133 square miles), the area holds immense strategic significance along the Shia pilgrimage route between the Iraqi capital and the holy city of Karbala.

It was once the site of former President Saddam Hussein’s military-industrial complexes, making its geography ideal for testing, building and concealing weapons.

Following the US-led invasion of Iraq in 2003 that toppled Hussein, it became a hotspot for armed confrontations before the ISIL (ISIS) armed group seized it in 2014. Later that year, the Iran-backed Popular Mobilisation Forces (PMF), an umbrella organisation of mostly Shia armed groups, recaptured the territory from ISIL.

Kataib Hezbollah, one of the largest groups within PMF, subsequently took full control, renaming the area Jurf al-Nasr and barring state institutions from entering. The militia sealed the town, citing security concerns, effectively preventing the return of approximately 140,000 displaced residents.

Last week, a leaked intelligence report said millions of dollars’ worth of crude oil had been siphoned from two state pipelines passing through the closed area since 2021. According to the document prepared by the Iraqi Ministry of Interior, the perpetrators allegedly constructed makeshift underground refineries to process the stolen resources.

The information led al-Zaidi to form a high-level investigative committee that entered the restricted zone on November 13 with military backing to confirm the existence of the illicit facilities. Earlier this week, the committee said it had identified several locations linked to smuggling operations in the area, without naming those allegedly implicated. As part of the anticorruption crackdown, nine senior security and administrative officials in Babil province, including the provincial police chief and the director of the Oil Pipelines Company, have also been dismissed.

According to the state Iraqi News Agency, the government has “ordered the armed forces to enter” Jurf al-Sakhar, setting a deadline “for the armed faction to exit the area”. Reports say the deadline for the withdrawal is Friday.

Kataib Hezbollah has denied the oil-smuggling allegations and, in harshly worded statements, accused al-Zaidi of corruption and framed the crackdown as a political extortion campaign. In a major show of force, the militia also mobilised approximately 8,000 fighters from various provinces towards Jurf al-Sakhar ahead of the government committee’s arrival.

Iraqi writer and journalist Hamza Mustafa told Al Jazeera that the military posturing masks underlying vulnerabilities. “What the brigades are doing through field mobilisation is perhaps the last line of defence for them after their position appeared weak regarding the oil-smuggling operations,” said Mustafa, noting that the previous narrative of fighting “terrorism” no longer held.

Security expert Saif Raad said the militia’s fierce resistance is driven by economics amid allegations that the restricted zone is also used to run thousands of illegal fish farms. “The desperation over this area is not for security reasons but for financial reasons,” said Raad, a former military officer.

Since taking office in May, al-Zaidi has made the disarmament of all armed factions in the country, including Kataib Hezbollah, a priority amid pressure from the United States, which has long demanded the decommissioning of the Iran-backed fighters. An initial September 30, 2026, deadline to bring all weapons under state control has since been pushed to June 2027.

“The issue here comes in the context of removing all pretexts from the armed factions after it was revealed that they are smuggling oil,” said Mustafa.

Fadel Abu Ragheef, an Iraqi political analyst, told Al Jazeera that al-Zaidi is in a distinctive position to take such unprecedented steps against entrenched interests. “He did not come from a partisan or bloc background, so his decisions are characterised by boldness and daring,” argued Abu Ragheef.

The standoff has deeply divided Iraq’s ruling Coordination Framework, prompting leaders such as Nouri al-Maliki, Hadi al-Amiri, Qais al-Khazali and Ammar al-Hakim to frantically mediate behind the scenes. Abu Ragheef suggested these factions are highly sensitive to issues such as disarmament.

“They harden their position if they hear the word disarmament or containment, so the concepts have shifted from disarmament and containment to organisation and management,” said Abu Ragheef, noting that the change has provided a crucial negotiating window until the June 2027 deadline.

With Friday’s deadline looming, Iran has also stepped in to avert a direct military clash. Esmail Qaani, commander of the Quds Force of the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps, headed to Baghdad to mediate the crisis and push for a solution. Qaani and al-Zaidi reportedly held talks until dawn on Tuesday, reaching a tentative agreement that would see Kataib Hezbollah withdraw “soon”.

Still, Mustafa warned that the crisis is not fully resolved.

“Qaani has not been able to dismantle the scene so far like he used to,” he said, referring to Iran’s historical influence, noting that Tehran had come to realise the issue is larger than expected due to al-Zaidi’s insistence.

Raad echoed this, emphasising al-Zaidi’s determination to centralise state arms, comparing it to his recent successful pacification of armed groups in the Sinjar district.

“The prime minister will not be prevented by Qaani or anyone else from going and restoring the authority of the commander in chief of the armed forces over all Iraqi territories,” he said. “This crisis is a beginning to restore the sovereign decision of the state.”

Israeli excavators demolished homes in Zawtar al-Sharqiye in southern Lebanon, one of the first pilot zones where the Lebanese army deployed under a framework agreement reached with Israel in June. Israel’s occupation has made large parts of the border region uninhabitable.

Acting US Navy Secretary Hung Cao made the remarks during a Senate Armed Services Committee confirmation hearing on Tuesday, as lawmakers questioned the cost of the war and its impact on freedom of navigation.

After the US and Israel launched strikes on Iran on February 28, Iran in effect closed the strait, allowing only some ships to pass while targeting those it says are unauthorised. This has raised the risks for shipping in the strait exponentially and caused severe shortages of oil, gas, fertiliser and other essential products from Gulf producers usually shipped via this route.

Cao’s claim has not been independently verified and challenges previously reported rises in insurance costs over the course of the nine-month-old conflict.

The remarks come as US President Donald Trump insists that the military campaign against Iran is effectively over, and that the US Navy is successfully escorting ships through the strait, even as new attacks on oil tankers and continued restrictions on shipping raise questions about whether one of the world’s most important energy waterways is really open.

The strait, the only sea route from the Gulf to the Arabian Sea and the open ocean beyond, carried about one-fifth of the world’s oil supplies before the war began.

Although some vessels are still navigating the waterway, shipping remains substantially below pre-war levels, while Iran and the US continue to impose competing restrictions.

During an exchange with Democratic Senator Elissa Slotkin, Cao said insurance costs for commercial vessels had risen dramatically since the conflict began.

He initially cited an insurance cost of $54,000 for a single crossing before clarifying that that was what insurance had previously cost, before the war. The cost now, he said, stood at $64m.

Slotkin responded by blaming the war for the increase, arguing that commercial vessels no longer enjoyed the same freedom of navigation they had before the conflict.

Cao also detailed the strain the war has placed on the US Navy, including prolonged deployments, deteriorating conditions and pressure on military resources.

“This war, again, I know it’s a strain on our navy,” he told lawmakers.

Democrats accused Cao of being a Trump “yes man” on the US-Israeli war on Iran, and downplaying its toll on sailors’ mental health after eight suicide attempts on an aircraft carrier.

Senator Kirsten Gillibrand, a Democrat from New York, asked him about a sailor who went overboard.

“Senator, that sailor was not trying to kill himself and he admitted that,” Cao told her, saying he used ‌a life preserver.

Gillibrand responded: “What was he trying to do? Swim to Guam?”

“I think you are minimising what mental health strain is on these service members,” Gillibrand replied, while dismissing Cao’s response as “inhumane”.

Cao’s $64m figure appears unusually high, even by the standards of wartime shipping insurance.

There is no independently verified evidence that $64m is the current insurance premium for a regular commercial vessel crossing the volatile strait.

“He gave no context. Is he talking about additional premiums for war risk insurance which are set as a percentage of hull value?” Michelle Bockmann, an analyst at maritime intelligence company Windward, told Al Jazeera.

“If so, it depends on the vessel type and the rate paid in order to get proper perspective.”

In July, a report published by S&P Global said that war-risk insurance premiums had climbed to between 7.5 and 10 percent of a ship’s hull value, compared with 1 to 3 percent previously.

It estimated that insurance for a tanker carrying 270,000 metric tonnes of crude could, therefore, cost approximately $21m.

Separately, Reuters news agency reported in September that the cost of moving an oil cargo through Hormuz had risen to roughly $10m-$20m, quoting an executive at Dubai’s Emirates National Oil Company (ENOC).

Regardless of whether it now costs $20m or $60m for insurance to transit the Strait of Hormuz, premiums have surged because ships face the possibility of being struck by missiles, drones or naval mines while passing through the waterway.

War-risk insurance covers vessels against losses arising from military conflict. Its price depends on the value of the vessel, the cargo and the likelihood of an attack.

Higher insurance costs can also feed into freight rates, fuel prices and the cost of goods transported around the world.

Technically, yes. But it remains far from fully and freely open as it was before the war.

Shipping traffic through the Strait of Hormuz remains approximately 65 percent below pre-war levels, according to the latest weekly report from the United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO).

The UKMTO recorded 308 vessel crossings during the seven days ending November 11, comprising 139 outbound and 169 inbound journeys.

Nevertheless, Trump has repeatedly suggested that Washington has secured shipping through the strait by providing naval escorts and maintaining the US naval blockade of Iranian ports.

Meanwhile, Iran insists that it, in fact, controls the passage of shipping through the strait.

Tehran has demanded that vessels use approved routes and coordinate with its forces. It has also announced exemptions for ships from India, China, Iraq and Qatar.

The route approved by Iran takes ships much closer to its own coastline than they used to sail, as the map below shows:

The continuing dangers to ships ignoring Iran’s warnings were demonstrated this week.

On Monday, UKMTO reported two tanker attacks, including one near Oman that left a vessel disabled and its engine room on fire. The following day, Iranian forces claimed three additional tankers had struck naval mines.

On Tuesday, the US attacked targets on Iran’s Qeshm island, near Hormuz, following an Iranian drone attack targeting US military installations in Bahrain in recent days.

Chris Beauchamp, chief market analyst at IG, said the strait could, therefore, hardly be considered open under normal circumstances.

“It is only open for business if mariners are prepared to take these risks, and it certainly isn’t open by any pre-war definition of the word,” he told Al Jazeera.

“It remains a miracle that we have avoided an energy crisis, and the longer this goes on, the more the alternatives will be developed.”

But Beauchamp said resolving the crisis would require Washington to confront the limits of its influence in the region.

“I can’t see a way that doesn’t involve conceding that the US does not have the ability to order things in the Middle East as it would wish,” he said.

news.originalContent:
(Photo by Elke Scholiers/Getty Images)

The White House won’t say whether President Donald Trump plans to oppose congressional efforts to expand military cooperation with Israel despite his pledge to end American financial assistance to the country.

Congress is racing to finalize the roughly $1.15 trillion fiscal 2027 National Defense Authorization Act (NDAA) during the lame-duck session, with the annual military policy bill still awaiting Senate action after passing the House in July, according to the Congressional Research Service. The legislation is among Congress’s major year-end priorities ahead of a Dec. 11 government funding deadline and the arrival of a new Democratic-controlled Congress in January.

The Daily Caller News Foundation asked the White House whether it supports removing three hotly debated Israel-related provisions from the final NDAA, how their inclusion aligns with Trump’s promise to end assistance and whether the administration has discussed their removal with congressional leadership. (RELATED: Swamp’s New Draft Defense Bill Would Open Up Billion-Dollar Taxpayer Purse For Foreign Countries)

(Photo by Jack GUEZ / AFP via Getty Images)

Trump announced on Nov. 3 that the United States would terminate approximately $4 billion in annual assistance to Israel by the end of the year, describing the financial arrangement as unnecessary during an appearance on “Fox & Friends,” according to the interview transcript.

Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu approached Trump months earlier about ending the assistance, the U.S. president said, adding that Israel could still purchase American weapons after the aid ends, according to the transcript.

The House-passed NDAA includes hundreds of millions of dollars for Israeli weapons programs, while the Senate’s version proposes expanding joint military research and manufacturing.

The White House has not clarified whether these expenditures would be affected by Trump’s promised aid cuts after multiple requests for comment.

Republicans’ sweeping defeat in the Nov. 3 midterm elections generated additional questions about the administration’s relationship with Israel, particularly after Vice President J.D. Vance publicly blamed the ongoing Iran War and American support for Israel for the party’s losses.

“The reason we lost is the war,” Vance wrote in a lengthy Nov. 4 X post.

One of the things the data analysts on our side obsessed over was "composition"—whether the electorate looked close enough to 2024 for Republicans to win. And despite polls that showed a Democrat blowout, the data kept on telling us the same story: in some states turnout was merely OK, in other states it was downright amazing, and in no state was it catastrophic. There was a genuine sense of optimism on our team: our people were showing up. So, I asked the smartest data guy I know, does that mean we’re going to shock the world? "No," he told me. "We might do better than the polls suggest. But the data is telling us that a lot of Trump/Vance 2024 voters are pissed and planning to vote for the other guys. Our voters are turning out, but they may not vote for us." Well, that looks prophetic now. Our voters did show up. In Florida, for example, the electorate was 9 points more Republican than Democrat, just a couple points worse than 2024. Undoubtedly there were places we could have done better on turnout. But the main problem is not turnout. The main problem is that many people who voted for Trump/Vance in 2024 voted for Democrats in 2026. There will be a lot of infighting and arguing over what happened and why that is. One of the pollsters I really respect told me that our economic messaging wasn’t sharp enough down the stretch. I’m sure that’s true. But the real reason we lost is obvious to almost everyone. Another pollster—one of the smartest people I know in politics, told me yesterday we’d lose the generic ballot by 13 points. I felt negative going into Tuesday, but even I was shocked by this. In his polling, he saw that a lot of Trump 2024 voters were angry and planning to vote for Democrats. He asked those voters who had abandoned us what would cause them to come back on our team. The top four answers, accounting for nearly all of the responses were: 1) End the war 2) Focus on cost of living/inflation 3) Put America First 4) Change our relationship to Israel Our voters showed up. And the above four reasons are why many of them voted for Democrats. This is according to a pollster who nailed the results. While many spent Monday attacking Rachel Campos Duffy for calling for a diplomatic resolution to the conflict, it turns out her political advice was sound. (She’s also a great person.) In the next few months, there’s going to be a lot of gaslighting. Expect to hear any number of establishment politicians say the solution to our woes is amnesty. I’m open to the idea that we should change enforcement—by focusing more on businesses that hire illegal labor, for instance. But anyone pushing amnesty is lying to you. The reason we lost is the war. The president himself said so last night. If you’d like to argue it was worth it, that losing the Senate for the next 6 years was worth it, then do so. Argue it was a worthwhile cost to pay. Agree or disagree, that’s at least honest. But everyone knows why we lost. And any honest conversation about where we go from here must start there. I remain hopeful about our country. To the people who are pissed off and want to say, “I told you so”: you’re right, you did tell us so. Take that energy into electing Republicans who share your worldview. To the people who are just pissed at the results, you should be. Let’s take that anger and get back to the work of saving our country.

Vance also cited inflation and a lack of focus on domestic priorities as concerns among disaffected Trump voters, according to his post.

A November poll found that 56% of registered voters opposed sending military aid to Israel, compared with 26% who supported it, according to YouGov. The survey sampled 3,166 registered voters from an opt-in panel between Nov. 4 and 6, weighted responses by demographic and political factors and had a margin of error of 2.2 percentage points, according to the pollster’s methodology.

Trump acknowledged growing public hostility toward Israel during a Nov. 8 interview with Ross Douthat on CBS’s “60 Minutes.”

“There’s a great dislike, incredibly, for Israel,” Trump said, adding that he didn’t disagree with Vance’s assessment, according to the transcript.

However, Trump defended the Iran strikes, claiming, “Israel would not exist except for Donald Trump,” according to the transcript. (RELATED: $1.15 Trillion In Defense Spending Approved By House Armed Services Committee)

Congress has already proposed $750 million in U.S.-Israeli defense cooperation through the House-passed FY2027 NDAA, a $65 million increase over fiscal 2026, according to AIPAC.

The funding includes $500 million for missile defense, $100 million each for counter-drone and subterranean warfare programs, and $50 million for emerging technologies, according to the legislation.

The missile defense funding includes $300 million for Israeli Cooperative Programs, $150 million for Arrow 3, $20 million for Iron Dome and $30 million for short-range ballistic missile defense, according to the House bill. (RELATED: Swamp’s Military-Industrial Complex Merger With Israel Inches Closer To Becoming Reality)

(Photo by DAVID FURST / AFP)

The proposed $750 million would fund joint U.S.-Israeli weapons development and military technology programs, rather than simply providing cash assistance to Israel. Congress must separately appropriate the money before it can be spent.

The spending dispute also involves a much larger financial relationship between the countries.

The current U.S.-Israel military assistance agreement provides for $38 billion over 10 years, including $33 billion in military financing and $5 billion in missile defense cooperation from fiscal 2019 through 2028, subject to congressional appropriations, according to the Congressional Research Service.

Trump’s announced termination of assistance at the end of 2026 would therefore precede the expiration of the existing agreement. Congress retains authority over federal appropriations, meaning the president’s announcement alone does not determine the fate of every existing assistance program, according to the Congressional Research Service.

The House Armed Services Committee approved the NDAA in a 44-12 vote in June despite objections over spending and expanded cooperation with Israel, according to the committee. The House passed the bill 216-212 on July 22, according to the Congressional Research Service.

The bill is currently being debated in a House-Senate conference committee.

The financial provisions are only one component of the proposed expansion.

Congress has also advanced legislation that would formally expand cooperation between American and Israeli defense industries, including joint weapons development and access to emerging military technologies.

Section 219 of the House-passed NDAA directs the Secretary of War to designate an executive agent responsible for coordinating bilateral defense technology research, development, testing and industrial cooperation. The provision would facilitate joint ventures, licensing agreements and American-based manufacturing partnerships involving Israeli companies.

The arrangement encompasses artificial intelligence, autonomous weapons, electronic warfare, directed-energy systems, cyber defense, biotechnology and other advanced military capabilities, according to the House bill.

The Senate’s Section 1217 proposes a similar arrangement through the United States-Israel Defense Technology Cooperation Initiative.

The legislation could more closely intertwine the countries’ defense industries and make it increasingly difficult for Washington to separate American military interests from Israeli priorities.

“Section 224 [now Section 219] would mark a fundamental shift in U.S.-Israel defense cooperation,” Ben Freeman, the director of Democratizing Foreign Policy at the Quincy Institute for Responsible Statecraft, previously told the DCNF. “In many areas, it would merge the U.S. and Israeli defense industrial bases.”

(Photo by Amir Levy/Getty Images)

Opposition has extended across party lines. (RELATED: Key Congressional Committee Reveals Extensive Waste In US Military Spending)

Republican Kentucky Rep. Thomas Massie and Democratic California Rep. Ro Khanna previously sought to remove the initiative, according to their proposed amendment. Khanna’s earlier attempt failed by voice vote, according to the committee.

“This is nothing more than codifying what has been happening for a long time,” Steven Bucci, a visiting fellow at the Heritage Foundation, previously told the DCNF. “This makes great sense.”

Such cooperation could continue benefiting American and Israeli defense firms despite Trump’s proposed aid cuts.

Twelve senators called for removing three NDAA provisions expanding military and intelligence cooperation with Israel in a Nov. 10 “dear colleague” letter, according to Democratic Maryland Sen. Chris Van Hollen’s office. The lawmakers targeted House Section 219, Senate Section 1217 and intelligence-sharing Section 618.

The intelligence provision would expand cooperation while restricting the administration’s ability to limit intelligence sharing without a national security justification, according to the Senate legislation.

The senators warned that the provisions could undermine U.S. independence, restrict Washington’s response to Israeli policies and shift military aid into less transparent defense contracts, according to their letter.

(Photo by JACK GUEZ/AFP via Getty Images)

The letter was signed by Van Hollen and 11 other lawmakers, including Democratic Massachusetts Sen. Elizabeth Warren, Democratic Washington Sen. Patty Murray, Democratic Oregon Sen. Ron Wyden, Democratic Illinois Sen. Tammy Duckworth and Independent Vermont Sen. Bernie Sanders.

The senators also pointed to Netanyahu’s expressed interest in replacing traditional American assistance with a broader defense partnership, questioning whether the proposed legislation could accomplish that objective without reducing Washington’s financial involvement.

The Senate letter also raised concerns about restrictions on the president’s discretion over intelligence sharing, particularly when the Israeli government’s actions conflict with American priorities. (RELATED: The Iran War Is Reportedly Bleeding The Pentagon Dry)

The White House has yet to clarify whether Trump’s promised aid cuts would affect the proposed $750 million in U.S.-Israeli defense cooperation.

The provisions remain under consideration as Congress reconciles the House and Senate NDAA proposals.

The House Armed Services Committee approved the NDAA in a 44-12 vote in June despite objections over spending and expanded cooperation with Israel, according to the committee. The House passed the bill 216-212 on July 22, according to the Congressional Research Service.

The bill is currently being debated in a House-Senate conference committee.

The financial provisions are only one component of the proposed expansion.

Congress has also advanced legislation that would formally expand cooperation between American and Israeli defense industries, including joint weapons development and access to emerging military technologies.

Section 219 of the House-passed NDAA directs the Secretary of War to designate an executive agent responsible for coordinating bilateral defense technology research, development, testing and industrial cooperation. The provision would facilitate joint ventures, licensing agreements and American-based manufacturing partnerships involving Israeli companies.

The arrangement encompasses artificial intelligence, autonomous weapons, electronic warfare, directed-energy systems, cyber defense, biotechnology and other advanced military capabilities, according to the House bill.

The Senate’s Section 1217 proposes a similar arrangement through the United States-Israel Defense Technology Cooperation Initiative.

The legislation could more closely intertwine the countries’ defense industries and make it increasingly difficult for Washington to separate American military interests from Israeli priorities.

“Section 224 [now Section 219] would mark a fundamental shift in U.S.-Israel defense cooperation,” Ben Freeman, the director of Democratizing Foreign Policy at the Quincy Institute for Responsible Statecraft, previously told the DCNF. “In many areas, it would merge the U.S. and Israeli defense industrial bases.”

(Photo by Amir Levy/Getty Images)

Opposition has extended across party lines. (RELATED: Key Congressional Committee Reveals Extensive Waste In US Military Spending)

Republican Kentucky Rep. Thomas Massie and Democratic California Rep. Ro Khanna previously sought to remove the initiative, according to their proposed amendment. Khanna’s earlier attempt failed by voice vote, according to the committee.

“This is nothing more than codifying what has been happening for a long time,” Steven Bucci, a visiting fellow at the Heritage Foundation, previously told the DCNF. “This makes great sense.”

Such cooperation could continue benefiting American and Israeli defense firms despite Trump’s proposed aid cuts.

Twelve senators called for removing three NDAA provisions expanding military and intelligence cooperation with Israel in a Nov. 10 “dear colleague” letter, according to Democratic Maryland Sen. Chris Van Hollen’s office. The lawmakers targeted House Section 219, Senate Section 1217 and intelligence-sharing Section 618.

The intelligence provision would expand cooperation while restricting the administration’s ability to limit intelligence sharing without a national security justification, according to the Senate legislation.

The senators warned that the provisions could undermine U.S. independence, restrict Washington’s response to Israeli policies and shift military aid into less transparent defense contracts, according to their letter.

(Photo by JACK GUEZ/AFP via Getty Images)

The letter was signed by Van Hollen and 11 other lawmakers, including Democratic Massachusetts Sen. Elizabeth Warren, Democratic Washington Sen. Patty Murray, Democratic Oregon Sen. Ron Wyden, Democratic Illinois Sen. Tammy Duckworth and Independent Vermont Sen. Bernie Sanders.

The senators also pointed to Netanyahu’s expressed interest in replacing traditional American assistance with a broader defense partnership, questioning whether the proposed legislation could accomplish that objective without reducing Washington’s financial involvement.

The Senate letter also raised concerns about restrictions on the president’s discretion over intelligence sharing, particularly when the Israeli government’s actions conflict with American priorities. (RELATED: The Iran War Is Reportedly Bleeding The Pentagon Dry)

The White House has yet to clarify whether Trump’s promised aid cuts would affect the proposed $750 million in U.S.-Israeli defense cooperation.

The provisions remain under consideration as Congress reconciles the House and Senate NDAA proposals.

news.originalContent:
The Trump administration pulled its nominee to lead the Food and Drug Administration (FDA), setting off a dispute over whether Senate Republicans or the Make America Healthy Again (MAHA) movement forced her out.

Heidi Overton, a physician and deputy director of the White House Domestic Policy Council, will now be replaced by another nominee as the White House seeks to advance its MAHA agenda, according to Axios.

“FDA nominee Heidi Overton lacks the support on the Hill to move forward with her confirmation,” a senior administration official told Axios late Tuesday.

“We need to go in a new direction at FDA, and everybody fully supports [Health] Secretary Kennedy’s vision to Make America Healthy Again and get back to a more populist and common-sense approach to health in America,” the official added, according to Axios.

Scoop: White House drops Heidi Overton’s FDA nomination https://t.co/CYriTACwk2

The White House’s move came at the last moment as the Senate health committee was due to vote on Overton’s nomination Wednesday, the New York Times reported.

Nominated by President Donald Trump in August, Overton underwent a Senate confirmation hearing in September. She had already drawn opposition from Democrats, some Republicans and some MAHA activists.

Republican Louisiana Sen. Bill Cassidy, the chair of the Senate Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions (HELP), had expressed “strong concerns” about the nomination back in August. Overton, he wrote, lacked the managerial experience required at an organization as large and beleaguered as the FDA.

“Additionally, Dr. Overton’s active role in last week’s nonsensical vaccine executive order calls into question her commitment to standing up for sound science and protecting children’s health. That alone is almost disqualifying,” he added.

Cassidy responded to the withdrawal by saying that Overton still had a “viable” path to confirmation.

“Tonight, the White House abandoned a viable confirmation path for Dr. Overton. The WH said that this was because she did not have the votes to pass. This was odd as I was having productive conversations with members. I believe she would have had the votes to pass out of committee and pass the full Senate.”

Overton helped draft and edit the scientific justification for revising the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention’s (CDC) childhood vaccine recommendations from 18 to 11—a justification that would inform President Trump’s executive order on childhood vaccinations, Semafor reported.

While a former senior administration official told Semafor that Overton drove the policy push, which was supported by Health Secretary and MAHA advocate Robert F. Kennedy Jr., another senior administration official said the push reflected the White House’s “top-down” approach and not Overton’s personal ideas.

Some influential MAHA advocates also questioned Overton’s nomination, alleging that she would side with health and agriculture interests and help undermine the MAHA agenda, according to Axios. (RELATED: EXCLUSIVE: Big Pharma Insider Backing RFK Jr.’s Pick To Lead FDA)

Alex Voetberg, née Clark, a prominent MAHA advocate, dismissed mainstream media reports that the withdrawal of Overton’s nomination had anything to do with Senate Republicans’ concerns, writing, “The explanation they’re looking for is the power of MAHA activists.”

“It’s remarkable how quickly the atmosphere in Washington can change. Susie Wiles is out. Stephen Miller is in. And almost immediately, we’re seeing movement on issues that MAGA and MAHA voters have been demanding action on for TWO YEARS. Now even Heidi Overton’s out for FDA,” she added.

Some pro-life advocates reportedly also doubted that Overton would tighten rules for prescribing the abortion pill mifepristone.

“This narrative took hold that Heidi was not aligned with Kennedy on this, was more aligned with pharma [on] vaccine stuff, and was in favor of a more maximal vaccine schedule,” the former senior administration official told Semafor. “And that’s just not the case, not what happened.”
